fields.title: The Key Teachings of John Wesley
fields.subtitle: An Ochorus companion to his life and teaching
fields.description: A concise, faithful guide to the heart of John Wesley’s message — salvation by faith, grace that goes before, the new birth, assurance, the means of grace and perfect love — and the conviction beneath it all: that the grace which pardons is the grace which heals. Nineteen short chapters, each ending in questions and a prayer, written by Ochorus as a companion to Wesley’s own public-domain works, which readers are warmly encouraged to go to directly.
fields.about_html:
This is not a book by John Wesley. It is a companion to him — an independent work of exposition and appreciation, written by Ochorus, that gathers the heart of his teaching into nineteen short chapters for the ordinary reader, with a chapter on his life, a conclusion and a guide to his books.

Wesley’s one theme was the recovery of love. He believed that sin is a disease of the whole person and that the gospel is God’s cure for it: grace that awakens before we seek, grace that pardons when we believe, and grace that goes on working until the love of God fills the heart and governs the life. From that single conviction came everything else — his preaching of the new birth and assurance, his insistence on prayer, Scripture and the Lord’s Supper, his small groups, his rules about money, his care for the sick and the poor, and his hatred of the slave trade. This volume follows that thread from the Epworth rectory to the fields and the class meeting, weighs honestly the places where he must be read with care, above all his teaching on Christian perfection, and ends each chapter in a few questions and a prayer.

Wesley’s own writings are in the public domain and freely available, and every chapter here names them so the reader can go to the source; A Plain Account of Christian Perfection and his Sermons on Several Occasions are in the Ochorus library. This companion is offered only to open the door. It quotes Scripture from the Authorised (King James) Version, and it makes no claim to stand in for the plain, urgent pages of the man himself.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
And we have known and believed the love that God hath to us. God is love; and he that dwelleth in love dwelleth in God, and God in him. 1 JOHN 4:16

John Wesley was an Oxford don who spent fifty years on horseback. He was a clergyman of the Church of England who preached in fields, market squares and graveyards because the pulpits were closed to him. He was a scholar who wrote grammars and a medical handbook and abridged whole libraries for poor readers, and he was a man who could stand before a mob with his hat knocked off and blood on his face and go on speaking about the love of God. When he died in 1791, the movement he had gathered had spread across Britain and Ireland and taken root in America, and it has since gone round the world.

One conviction beneath the rest

His message can be put in a sentence. The grace that pardons is the grace that heals. Wesley believed that human beings were made in the image of God, that sin has defaced that image in every part of us, and that the gospel is God’s way of restoring it. He did not think of salvation chiefly as a ticket to heaven, though he believed in heaven with all his heart. He thought of it as a cure. God forgives the guilt of sin, and in the same moment begins to break its power, and He does not stop until love for Him and for our neighbour fills the heart and rules the life.

Ye shall be holy: for I the LORD your God am holy. LEVITICUS 19:2

Almost everything he taught follows from this. There is grace before we seek God, stirring conscience and drawing us to Him; Wesley called it preventing grace, the grace that goes before. There is grace that justifies, received by faith alone, and with it a new birth and an inward witness that we are children of God. And there is grace that sanctifies, working through prayer and Scripture and the Lord’s Supper, through fellowship and works of mercy, until the believer is, in his favourite phrase, made perfect in love. His teaching on money, on the poor, on the slave trade and on Christian unity is not a separate department. It is the same love, carried into the street and the counting-house.

Why he still matters

Wesley is worth reading for at least three reasons.

The first is that he refused to separate faith from holiness. He preached justification by faith alone as plainly as Luther, and he preached the pursuit of holiness as earnestly as any Puritan, and he would not let either swallow the other. A faith that did not make people more loving was not, in his judgement, the faith of the New Testament.

The second is that he wrote for ordinary people. In the preface to his sermons he says that he designed plain truth for plain people, and he meant it. He stripped his sermons of learned display, and the result is prose that a farmer or a factory hand could follow, and that still reads with remarkable clarity.

The third is that he made the Christian life a shared life. He did not leave converts alone with their feelings. He put them into small groups, gave them rules, set them to visit the sick and the imprisoned, and asked them every week how their souls were prospering. Whatever else Christians today learn from him, they may learn that holiness is not a private hobby.

How this book is arranged

After a chapter on his life, nineteen short chapters set out his teaching. They follow what he called the scripture way of salvation: from the faith that saves and the danger of being only almost a Christian, through the disease of sin and the grace that goes before, to justification, the new birth and the witness of the Spirit. They go on to sin in believers, the way of sanctification, Christian perfection and what it does not mean, and then to the practical life he built on those foundations: the means of grace, works of piety and mercy, the class meeting, the use of money, the catholic spirit, the call to the fields, and his care for the poor and the enslaved.

Each chapter ends with application points and a prayer. Wesley would have approved. His brother Charles gave the movement its hymns, and John saw to it that Methodists sang, prayed and examined themselves as well as listened. Read a chapter a day, or one a week. Stop at the application points. Pray the prayer, or better, pray your own.

Where he must be read with care

This is not a book of hero-worship, and it is better to say at the outset where Wesley must be weighed rather than simply received.

His teaching on Christian perfection has been misunderstood from his day to ours, sometimes by his friends as much as his enemies. He did not teach that a Christian could become sinless, free from mistakes or beyond temptation, and he said so repeatedly. But his language could run ahead of his qualifications, and some who followed him claimed more than he did and fell into pride and delusion. Chapters thirteen and fourteen set out what he taught and where it needs care.

Second, his quarrel with George Whitefield over predestination divided the revival. Wesley was sincerely convinced that the doctrine as he understood it dishonoured God, and his sermon Free Grace says so with force. But he was not always fair to what careful Calvinists actually believed, and many of his Reformed brothers have served Christ as faithfully as he did. Chapter seven tries to set out the dispute honestly.

Third, he governed his movement with a firm, sometimes autocratic hand. He appointed and removed preachers, set the rules and interpreted them, and did not easily share authority. It served the movement in its early years and cost it later. And his own marriage was unhappy, as the biographical chapter says plainly.

Why read him, then? Because on the central matter he was right. God does not merely forgive us and leave us as we were. He means to make us whole. The counsel of this book is the counsel of Scripture: Prove all things; hold fast that which is good (1 Thessalonians 5:21). Where Wesley is faithful — on grace, on faith, on assurance, on love — receive it gladly and act on it. Where he presses beyond what is written, set it aside and lose nothing.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Ask yourself honestly whether you think of salvation mainly as forgiveness, mainly as a change of life, or as both together.

2. Choose a pace for this book — a chapter a day or a chapter a week — and decide now when you will read it.

3. Name one person with whom you could share what you learn, and perhaps read these chapters alongside.

4. Resolve to test everything in these pages against Scripture, keeping what is true and setting aside what is not.

5. Ask God to use this book to send you not to Wesley but to Christ, and to love.

A PRAYER
Gracious God, You made us in Your image, and You have not given us up though we have marred it.
Thank You for Your grace, which went before me when I was not seeking You, which pardons me through the blood of Jesus, and which is able to make me new.
As I read of Your servant John Wesley, keep me from admiring a man and missing his Master. Where he is faithful to Your Word, let me receive it; where he is not, give me discernment.
Fill my heart with Your love, and let that love rule my life, for the sake of Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

fields.title: A Brand Plucked out of the Burning
fields.body_html:
Is not this a brand plucked out of the fire? ZECHARIAH 3:2

The rectory at Epworth. John Wesley was born in June 1703 at Epworth in Lincolnshire, the fifteenth child of Samuel Wesley, the rector, and his wife Susanna. Samuel was a learned, difficult, frequently indebted clergyman who never quite won the affection of his parishioners. Susanna was one of the remarkable women of her century: devout, formidably intelligent, and the architect of a household run with a discipline that her son would later carry into a nation. Of her many children fewer than half lived to grow up. She taught those who did in a schoolroom at home, with fixed hours, and set aside time each week to speak with each child alone about their soul.

The fire. On the night of 9 February 1709 the rectory burned. The family escaped into the garden, and only then realised that John, not yet six, had been left asleep upstairs. He appeared at a window with the roof alight above him. There was no time to fetch a ladder; neighbours climbed on one another’s shoulders and pulled him out, and moments later the roof fell in. His mother took the rescue as a sign that God had a purpose for him, and she resolved to take particular care of his soul. Wesley himself came to use the words of Zechariah about his escape: a brand plucked out of the burning. It became the phrase of his life.

Oxford and the Holy Club. He was educated at Charterhouse School in London and at Christ Church, Oxford, which he entered in 1720. In 1725, reading Jeremy Taylor’s Holy Living and Dying and then Thomas à Kempis, he resolved to give his whole life to God; William Law’s Christian Perfection and A Serious Call followed and deepened the resolve. He was ordained deacon in 1725, elected a Fellow of Lincoln College in 1726, and ordained priest in 1728. Back in Oxford he took the lead of a small group his younger brother Charles had gathered for prayer, study of the Scriptures, weekly Communion, fasting, and visits to prisoners and the poor. The university laughed at them. Among the nicknames was the one that stuck: Methodists, for their methodical piety. The young George Whitefield joined them.

Georgia. In October 1735 John and Charles sailed for the new colony of Georgia, John to serve as a minister to the settlers and, he hoped, to preach to the native peoples. On the voyage a violent storm broke over the ship, and while the English passengers screamed, a company of German Moravians went on singing their psalm. Wesley was afraid to die, and he knew it. He asked one of them afterwards whether he had not been afraid, and was told that he was not, and that the women and children were not afraid either. The mission itself went badly. Wesley was rigid and unwise, his pastoral care of a young woman named Sophy Hopkey became an entanglement he could neither commit to nor end, and after she married another man a legal dispute followed his refusal of Communion to her. He left the colony at the end of 1737, humbled and convinced that he had gone to convert others and had never been converted himself.

Aldersgate. Back in London he met another Moravian, Peter Böhler, who told him plainly that he lacked the faith that brings assurance, and counselled him to go on preaching faith until he had it. On the evening of 24 May 1738 he went, unwillingly, to a society meeting in Aldersgate Street, where someone was reading Luther’s preface to the Epistle to the Romans. His Journal records what happened. “I felt my heart strangely warmed. I felt I did trust in Christ, Christ alone, for salvation.” He received that night not a new doctrine but assurance: the knowledge that his sins, even his, had been taken away. Within weeks he preached before the University of Oxford on the text By grace are ye saved through faith. The sermon, Salvation by Faith, stands first in his collected sermons.

Into the fields. Whitefield had begun preaching in the open air to the colliers near Bristol and begged Wesley to come and take up the work. Wesley recoiled. He had been so attached to church order, he later admitted, that he would once have thought the saving of souls almost a sin if it had not been done in a church. On 2 April 1739 he preached in a field outside Bristol to some thousands of people. The pulpits of the Church of England were closing against him, and when he was challenged for preaching in other men’s parishes, his Journal records his answer: “I look upon all the world as my parish.” From then until his old age he travelled almost ceaselessly, usually on horseback, rising early and preaching often at five in the morning to workers on their way to the pits and mills. The traditional figures, some quarter of a million miles and forty thousand sermons, are later estimates rather than his own tallies, but his Journal leaves no doubt of the scale.

Societies and classes. His genius, as many have said, was less in the pulpit than in what came after it. He gathered those who were awakened into societies, and in 1742 the societies were divided into classes of about a dozen, each under a leader who met them weekly. From 1744 he met his preachers, many of them laymen, in an annual Conference. He wrote, abridged and published constantly, from sermons and hymns to a Christian Library of devotional classics, a book of simple remedies for the poor, and notes on the New Testament. Charles wrote the hymns, several thousand of them, and the people sang their theology.

Opposition and division. The early years brought mobs, and Wesley learned to face a hostile crowd with a calm that often disarmed it. They brought controversy too. His sermon Free Grace, an attack on predestination, divided the revival into Arminian and Calvinist streams and wounded Whitefield; yet the friendship survived, and when Whitefield died in 1770 it was Wesley who preached his funeral sermon in London.

Marriage. In 1751 he married Mary Vazeille, a widow. The marriage was unhappy from early on and remained so. He would not travel less, and she resented his absences and his correspondence with women in the societies; she left him more than once, and they lived apart for years before her death in 1781. The man who guided thousands could not order his own house, and honesty requires that it be said.

The last years. He never meant to leave the Church of England and never formally did. But in 1784 he made legal provision for the Conference to hold the chapels after his death, and in the same year, since the American Methodists had no bishops willing to serve them, he ordained ministers for America himself, a step that made separation all but certain. He kept preaching into his eighties. In the last days of his life he wrote to encourage William Wilberforce in the campaign against the slave trade. He died at his house beside the City Road Chapel in London on 2 March 1791, in his eighty-eighth year. Those round his bed remembered him saying more than once, “The best of all is, God is with us.” He left very little money. He had given it away, as he had taught others to do.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Wesley was a disciplined, devout clergyman for years before he knew the assurance of forgiveness. Ask whether your own religion rests on your effort or on Christ.

2. The calm of the Moravians in the storm exposed his fear. What recent trial has exposed where your trust really lies?

3. He preached faith before he felt it, on the advice of a younger man. Is there someone God has sent to tell you something you did not want to hear?

4. Wesley overcame his dislike of field preaching for the sake of people who would never enter a church. What preference of yours might God be asking you to lay down for others?

5. Choose one of Wesley’s sermons in the Ochorus library, Salvation by Faith or The Almost Christian, and read it this week.

A PRAYER
Lord God, You plucked Your servant out of the burning and kept him for Your purpose. You have kept me too, often when I did not know it.
Forgive me for trying to earn what You give freely. Warm my heart with the assurance that Christ died for me, even for me.
Give me courage to go where people are, and not only where I am comfortable.
Where my life, like his, is marked by failure at home or in the work, humble me and heal what can be healed. And let me say at the last, with him, that the best of all is that You are with us. Amen.

fields.title: Salvation by Faith
fields.body_html:
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast. EPHESIANS 2:8–9

On 18 June 1738, less than four weeks after Aldersgate, John Wesley stood in the pulpit of St Mary’s, Oxford, before the university that had laughed at the Holy Club, and preached on this text. He had spent thirteen years trying to make himself holy enough for God. Now he told the most learned audience in England that salvation was a gift. When he later gathered his sermons into a collection, he put this one first. Everything else he preached stands on it.

Grace the source, faith the condition

fields.body_html:
Then Agrippa said unto Paul, Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian. ACTS 26:28

On 25 July 1741 Wesley preached again before the University of Oxford, and chose for his text the words of King Agrippa to Paul. It is one of his most searching sermons, and one of his most personal, for the portrait he paints of the almost Christian is in large part a portrait of himself before 1738. He had been, he tells his hearers, that man for many years. He had done everything in the sermon’s first half and lacked everything in its second.

How far a person may go

Wesley’s method is to build up the almost Christian piece by piece, until the hearer is uncomfortable at how much it includes.

First, he says, there is heathen honesty: the ordinary justice, truthfulness and kindness that even pagan societies expected. The almost Christian does not steal, cheat or oppress the poor. He tells the truth and helps his neighbour when he can.

Second, there is the form of godliness, the whole outside of a real Christian. The almost Christian does nothing the gospel forbids. He does not take God’s name in vain, profane the Lord’s day, indulge in drunkenness or quarrel. He does good to all, feeds the hungry and comforts the afflicted. He goes to church and behaves there with seriousness. He comes to the Lord’s table. He prays with his family and alone.

Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away. 2 TIMOTHY 3:5

Third, and this is the sting, the almost Christian has sincerity. He is not a hypocrite. He has a real design to serve God and a hearty desire to do His will. Wesley insists on this. A person may go so far as to mean it, and still be only almost a Christian.

The confession in the pulpit

At this point Wesley does something striking. He anticipates the objection that no one could go so far and yet fall short, and he answers it from his own life. He had gone thus far for many years, he says, as many in the room could testify: using diligence to avoid evil and keep a conscience void of offence, redeeming the time, using every means of grace, doing all the good he could, and all of it with a sincere desire to serve God. And yet his own conscience, he says, bore him witness that all this time he was only almost a Christian.

It is not hard to imagine the effect. Wesley had been a Fellow of Lincoln College, a leader of the Holy Club, and a missionary. His hearers knew his reputation for strictness. Now he told them that it had not been enough, and invited them to ask whether their own religion was any different.

What it means to be altogether a Christian

The second half of the sermon describes the altogether Christian, and it rests on three things.

The first is the love of God. Wesley takes the great commandment at full strength: to love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and soul, and mind, and strength. Such love, he says, engrosses the whole heart and takes up all the affections. The one who has it rejoices in God his Saviour, and is crucified to the world.

And thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind, and with all thy strength: this is the first commandment. MARK 12:30

The second is the love of our neighbour, which means every person in the world, including our enemies. Wesley describes it through Paul’s words in First Corinthians thirteen: it is longsuffering and kind, envies not, is not puffed up, seeks not its own, thinks no evil, and bears, believes, hopes and endures all things.

The third is the ground of both, which is faith. Here Wesley quotes the Homilies of the Church of England at length, insisting that the faith which does not bring forth repentance, love and good works is not a living faith but a dead one. True Christian faith, in the Homily’s words, is a sure trust and confidence in God that by the merits of Christ one’s sins are forgiven, and from it follows a loving heart to obey His commandments. Whoever has this faith working by love, Wesley concludes, “is not almost only, but altogether, a Christian.”

For in Jesus Christ neither circumcision availeth any thing, nor uncircumcision; but faith which worketh by love. GALATIANS 5:6

The questions at the end

The sermon closes with a series of questions that Wesley plainly meant his hearers to answer in their hearts, and that still do their work. Do I practise even the justice and truth that the heathen require? Do I have the form of godliness? Do I have sincerity? And then the great question: “Is the love of God shed abroad in your heart?” Can you cry out, My God, and my all? Do you love your neighbour as yourself, and your enemies, as Christ loved you? Do you believe that Christ loved you and gave himself for you? Does His Spirit bear witness with yours that you are a child of God?

And hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us. ROMANS 5:5

Reading it without despair

This sermon has sent many people into anxiety, and it is worth saying how to read it well.

Wesley was preaching to an audience that was, for the most part, comfortable in a religion of respectability. He meant to disturb them, and he was right to. But the answer he gives is not more effort. The almost Christian already has plenty of effort. What he lacks is the love of God, and that is not something he can manufacture. It is shed abroad in the heart by the Holy Spirit, and it comes through faith in Christ. The sermon ends not with a demand but with an invitation: to cry to God day and night until you know in whom you have believed.

I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day. 2 TIMOTHY 1:12

The tender conscience that reads this sermon and concludes that it can never be good enough has understood half of it. The whole of it says: you were never meant to be good enough. You were meant to believe and to be loved, and to love in return.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Read through Wesley’s three marks of the almost Christian — honesty, the form of godliness, sincerity — and ask which of them you rely on for your standing with God.

2. Ask yourself his great question slowly: is the love of God shed abroad in my heart? Write down what you honestly find.

3. Name one enemy or difficult person, and pray for their good by name this week.

4. If you have been comfortable in a religion of respectability, tell God so plainly, and ask Him for a living faith.

5. If you have been anxious that you can never do enough, read the last paragraphs of The Almost Christian and rest in the invitation rather than the demand.

A PRAYER
Lord, You know how far I have gone in the outward forms of religion, and how easily I can mistake them for the life of faith.
Search my heart. If I am only almost a Christian, do not let me rest there.
Shed abroad Your love in my heart by the Holy Spirit. Give me faith that trusts Christ alone, and let that faith work by love to You and to every person, even my enemies.
Let me not be content with good intentions, but bring them to good effect by Your grace. Amen.

fields.title: The Disease and the Physician
fields.body_html:
And GOD saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually. GENESIS 6:5

Wesley is often remembered as the optimist of the evangelical revival, the preacher who believed that grace could do great things in human lives. That is true. But his optimism about grace was built on a thorough pessimism about human nature, and no one who skips the second will understand the first. His sermon Original Sin, preached on the text above, is one of the bleakest things he wrote. It is also one of the most hopeful, because it ends by describing religion as a cure.

Against the flattering view of man

Wesley wrote at a time when many educated people, inside the church and out, spoke warmly of human nature. The moral philosophers of the age described people as naturally benevolent, reasonable and inclined to virtue. Wesley thought this was not only false but dangerous. If we are not sick, we will not look for a physician.

So he set out to describe human nature as Scripture describes it, and he began with the generation of the flood. God saw that every imagination of the thoughts of man’s heart was only evil continually. Wesley asks whether this is true of humanity now, and answers that it is. By nature, he argues, every person is without the true knowledge of God and without the love of God. Men may speak of a God, but in practice they live as though there were none. They are, in the apostle’s phrase, without God in the world.

Wherefore remember, that ye being in time past Gentiles in the flesh … were without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world. EPHESIANS 2:11–12

The symptoms

Wesley then diagnoses the disease by its symptoms, much as a physician would. And he was interested in medicine; he wrote a popular book of remedies for the poor.

The first symptom is practical atheism: we do not know God and do not seek Him. The second is idolatry, not of carved images but of ourselves. We set up self in the place of God, and pride follows. The third is self-will, the determination to have our own way, in which, Wesley says, Satan has stamped his own image on our hearts. The fourth is the love of the world in all its forms: what John calls the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life.

For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world. 1 JOHN 2:16

Wesley’s treatment of the pride of life is especially sharp. He points out that the desire for the praise of others is so natural to us that we call it a virtue. Even eminent Christians, he says, think it a mark of a wicked mind not to care what others think of us. And yet Jesus asked how those can believe who receive honour one of another, and seek not the honour that cometh from God only.

The dividing line

From this dark picture Wesley draws a conclusion that is still bracing. Original sin, he says, is the first grand distinguishing point between heathenism and Christianity. The best pagan moralists described the vices of particular people, and some of them described vice very well. But none of them knew that the whole of human nature is fallen, that every faculty is disordered, that we are born turned away from God. Anyone who denies this, he says, is a heathen still in the fundamental point, whatever else he believes.

Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me. PSALM 51:5

Religion as healing

And now the turn. Having described the disease, Wesley describes the cure, and his definition of religion here is one of the most beautiful he gave. The religion of Jesus Christ, he says, is “God’s method of healing a soul which is thus diseased.” He uses a Greek phrase for it, therapeia psyches, the therapy or healing of the soul.

The great Physician of souls, he goes on, applies His medicines to every part of the sickness. He heals our practical atheism by the knowledge of Himself and of Jesus Christ, giving us faith, and in particular the conviction that Christ loved me and gave Himself for me. He heals our pride by repentance and lowliness of heart. He heals our self-will by resignation, a meek and thankful submission to His will. And for the love of the world in all its branches, the love of God is the sovereign remedy.

This is the whole of Wesley’s theology in miniature. Salvation is not merely a change in our legal standing, though it is that. It is the restoration of a ruined nature, the renewal of the image of God in which we were made. Any religion that stops short of the renewal of the soul in the image of God is, he says in the same sermon, no better than a poor farce and a mockery of God.

Wesley’s diagnosis also explains why he preached so urgently. In the sermon Awake, Thou That Sleepest, which his brother Charles preached at Oxford in 1742 and which is printed among John’s sermons, the sleeper is described as a sinner satisfied in his sins, content to remain in his fallen state, ignorant both of his disease and of the only remedy for it.

A sick man who does not know he is sick will not send for the doctor. That is why Wesley’s preaching so often began with conviction of sin. He did not enjoy making people miserable. He wanted them well.

Wesley’s picture of fallen humanity is severe, and some readers will find it too much. It is worth remembering two things. fields.body_html:
That was the true Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world. JOHN 1:9

If the last chapter left the reader in the dark, Wesley would not have left him there long. His sermon Original Sin describes humanity as it would be in a state of mere nature, entirely without God. But he did not believe that anyone actually lives in that state. Between our ruin and our salvation he placed a teaching that is one of the most distinctive and most pastorally important things he gave the church. He called it preventing grace, using the old sense of the word prevent, to come before. We would call it prevenient grace: the grace that goes before.

No one is left in mere nature

The fullest statement comes in a late sermon, On Working Out Our Own Salvation. Wesley grants everything he said about the fall. All human souls are dead in sin by nature. We cannot quicken ourselves, any more than a dead body can raise itself. And yet, he says, this excuses no one, because there is no one who is in a state of mere nature. Unless he has quenched the Spirit, no one is wholly void of the grace of God.

What people commonly call natural conscience, he goes on, is not natural at all. “It is more properly termed preventing grace.” Everyone has some measure of it. Everyone has, sooner or later, good desires, though most stifle them before they take root. Everyone has some faint glimmering of that light which enlightens every man that cometh into the world. And everyone, unless his conscience is seared, feels uneasy when he acts against it.

Then comes a sentence that Wesley’s hearers would not easily forget: “no man sins because he has not grace, but because he does not use the grace which he hath.”

For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men. TITUS 2:11

The first dawn of salvation

In the same sermon Wesley sets out the whole course of salvation, and preventing grace stands at its beginning. Salvation, he says, begins with “the first wish to please God, the first dawn of light concerning his will, and the first slight transient conviction of having sinned against him.” These are small things, but they are not nothing. They imply some tendency toward life, the beginning of a deliverance from a blind and unfeeling heart.

Salvation goes on by convincing grace, which Scripture calls repentance, bringing deeper self-knowledge. Then comes what Wesley calls the proper Christian salvation, with its two branches of justification and sanctification. By justification we are saved from the guilt of sin and restored to God’s favour; by sanctification we are saved from the power and root of sin and restored to God’s image.

No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day. JOHN 6:44

In The Scripture Way of Salvation he describes the same beginning in almost the same words. If salvation is taken in its widest sense, he says, it includes all the drawings of the Father, all the desires after God which increase if we yield to them, all the light with which the Son enlightens every person, and all the convictions His Spirit works in every child of man, though most people try to forget them.

God works, therefore you can work

The text of On Working Out Our Own Salvation is from Philippians, and Wesley’s handling of it is a model of how he held grace and responsibility together.

Wherefore, my beloved, as ye have always obeyed, not as in my presence only, but now much more in my absence, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure. PHILIPPIANS 2:12–13

Christians have often set these two verses against each other, as though the second meant we have nothing to do and the first that everything depends on us. Wesley insists that there is no opposition between them. God works, therefore you can work; if He did not, it would be impossible. And God works, therefore you must work: we are to be workers together with Him, otherwise, he warns, He will cease working. He quotes Augustine, the great teacher of grace: “He that made us without ourselves, will not save us without ourselves.”

This is the balance that runs through all Wesley’s teaching. Everything good in us is God’s gift, from the first flicker of conscience to the last perfection of love. But the gift is not forced on us. God works in us, and we are to work it out.

Why it matters

Preventing grace was Wesley’s answer to two errors at once.

Against those who flattered human nature, he held that we can do nothing good of ourselves. Every good desire, every stirring of conscience, is God’s gift. In this he stood with Augustine, Luther and Calvin. He never taught that people could save themselves or even begin to turn to God unaided.

Against those who taught that God gives saving grace to some and withholds it from others, he held that grace is given to all. This is where he parted company with his Calvinist friends, as the next chapter explains. For Wesley, the reason some are lost is not that God passed them by but that they resisted the grace He gave them.

Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me. REVELATION 3:20

It also shaped his evangelism. Wesley preached to colliers, prisoners, drunkards and condemned men on the assumption that God was already at work in them. He was looking for the good desires that had not yet been stifled, the conscience not yet seared. His confidence that every person he met had some glimmer of divine light made him hopeful about people others had written off.

Where to read with care

The doctrine can be misused. A person may take comfort in having a conscience and good desires, as though these were enough. Wesley would have been horrified. Preventing grace is the beginning of salvation, not its substance; it is the dawn, not the day. Its whole purpose is to lead to repentance and faith in Christ. The one who has felt God’s drawing and resisted it is not safer for having felt it.

Readers in the Reformed tradition will also want to ask whether Wesley’s account is the best reading of passages such as John 6:44. They are entitled to. What should be granted on all sides is that Wesley, like his opponents, gave God all the glory for every good thing in the human heart.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Recall the first stirrings of desire for God in your own life. Thank Him that He was at work before you were seeking Him.

2. Is there a present conviction of conscience that you have been stifling? Stop resisting it today.

3. Think of someone you have written off as beyond reach. Ask God to show you where His light may already be glimmering in them.

4. Take the words God works, therefore you can work; God works, therefore you must work, and apply them to one duty you have been neglecting.

5. Read On Working Out Our Own Salvation in Wesley’s Sermons on Several Occasions in the Ochorus library.

A PRAYER
Father, You loved me before I loved You, and You drew me before I came.
Thank You for every good desire, every stirring of conscience and every glimmer of light that You have given me. Forgive me for the times I have stifled them.
Work in me both to will and to do of Your good pleasure, and give me grace to work out what You are working in.
And let me look on every person as one to whom You have already come, and in whom Your light is shining. Amen.

fields.title: Free Grace
fields.body_html:
He that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things? ROMANS 8:32

This is the chapter in which Wesley must be handled most carefully, because it concerns a quarrel between good men. In the first years of the revival Wesley preached at Bristol, and then published, a sermon called Free Grace. It was an attack on the doctrine of predestination as taught by many of his fellow evangelicals, and above all by his friend George Whitefield, whose preaching had done so much to begin the awakening. The sermon split the revival into two streams, and the division has never fully healed. It deserves to be understood, both for what Wesley was defending and for what he got wrong.

Free in all, and free for all

The positive heart of the sermon is a single phrase, and it is a noble one. “The grace or love of God, whence cometh our salvation, is FREE IN ALL, and FREE FOR ALL.”

Free in all, Wesley explains, means that grace does not depend on any power or merit in the person who receives it. It does not depend on good works, or good tempers, or good desires, or even on faith considered as our own achievement. All these are the fruits of grace, not its cause. Whatever good is in anyone, God is the author of it.

For who maketh thee to differ from another? and what hast thou that thou didst not receive? now if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory, as if thou hadst not received it? 1 CORINTHIANS 4:7

On this point Wesley and Whitefield were entirely agreed. Both preached salvation by grace alone through faith alone, and both gave God all the glory.

Free for all, Wesley goes on, is where they parted. Wesley believed that God’s saving grace is offered to every human being without exception, that Christ died for all, and that no one is lost because God decreed it, but only because he refused the grace that was given him. He held that the doctrine of an eternal decree, by which some are chosen for salvation and the rest passed over, could not be squared with this.

For this is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Saviour; Who will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth. 1 TIMOTHY 2:3–4

Wesley’s arguments

The body of the sermon is a list of objections to predestination, pressed with all Wesley’s logical force. If the number of the saved is fixed from eternity, he argues, then preaching is in vain, since it can change nothing. The doctrine tends to destroy holiness, because it removes the motives Scripture offers, the hope of reward and the fear of punishment. It tends to destroy the comfort of religion, since no one can be sure he is elect. It tends to destroy zeal for good works, and especially for doing good to the souls of others. It sets Scripture against itself, since the Bible is full of universal invitations and warnings.

The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance. 2 PETER 3:9

And then, in the most notorious passage, Wesley says that the doctrine is full of blasphemy, because it represents the most holy God as worse than the devil, more false, more cruel and more unjust. He adds that he loves the persons who hold it even while he abhors the doctrine, and he asks his readers to pray for them. But the words were said, and they wounded.

Where he was right

Wesley was defending something precious. He could not bear the thought that any human being might be told, in effect, that the gospel was not for him. He had seen the despair of people who feared they were not among the elect, and he had seen others grow careless on the assumption that they were. His whole ministry rested on the conviction that he could say to anyone, in any field or prison, that Christ died for you.

Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. MATTHEW 11:28

His insistence that God’s love is real toward every person, and that the invitations of Scripture are sincere, is a word the whole church needs. So is his conviction that the doctrine of election must never be used to excuse sin or to make evangelism seem pointless.

Where he was unfair

But he was not fair to his opponents, and honesty requires that this be said plainly.

Wesley argued as though his opponents’ doctrine must lead to the consequences he drew from it, and then charged them with those consequences. But Whitefield and the careful Calvinists of the day did not believe that preaching was vain; they preached with a zeal that equalled Wesley’s. They did not think holiness unnecessary; many of them were among the holiest people of the century. They did not believe God was cruel; they believed that He was just in condemning sinners and wonderfully merciful in saving any. Whitefield answered in a published letter, firm but affectionate, arguing that Wesley had misrepresented the doctrine he attacked.

It must also be said that the Calvinists’ reading of passages such as Romans nine and Ephesians one is a serious reading, held by some of the most careful interpreters in the history of the church, and not simply a failure to see what is obvious. Wesley’s own reading has its difficulties as well as its strengths.

Having predestinated us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will. EPHESIANS 1:5

The friendship that survived

The best part of this story is how it ended. Wesley and Whitefield did not agree, but they did not stop loving each other. They came to an understanding that allowed each to preach in his own way, and in later years the old affection was openly renewed. When Whitefield died in America in 1770, it was Wesley who preached his funeral sermon in London, and it is printed among Wesley’s collected sermons.

In it Wesley sums up the doctrines his friend everywhere insisted on, and he does it in two phrases they held in common: “the new birth, and justification by faith”. He urges his hearers to keep close to these good, old, unfashionable doctrines, and even more to drink into Whitefield’s spirit. It is a generous sermon. It is also a model for Christians who disagree on questions of this kind: hold your convictions, argue them honestly, and do not let them cost you your love for a brother.

Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. EPHESIANS 4:3
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Thank God that His grace is free in all: that nothing in you earned it, not even your faith.

2. Whatever your view of election, ask whether you speak to others as though the gospel is truly for them.

3. Think of a Christian with whom you disagree on an important doctrine. Pray for them by name and thank God for their faithfulness.

4. If you have ever argued against a view by charging its holders with consequences they reject, consider how you might state their view fairly.

5. Read Free Grace and Wesley’s sermon on the death of Whitefield together, and notice the difference in tone.

A PRAYER
Father, You spared not Your own Son, but gave Him up for us all. Thank You that Your grace is free, and that nothing in me deserved it.
Give me Wesley’s longing that every person should hear that Christ died for them, and give me more charity than he sometimes showed to those who see these things differently.
Keep me from turning doctrine into a weapon against my brothers and sisters.
Let me hold the truth firmly and love Your people warmly, until we all see face to face. Amen.

ROMANS 8:32 This is the chapter in which Wesley must be handled most carefully, because it concerns a quarrel between good men. In the first years of the revival Wesley preached at Bristol, and then published, a sermon called Free Grace. It does not depend on good works, or good tempers, or good desires, or even on faith considered as our own achievement. All these are the fruits of grace, not its cause. Whatever good is in anyone, God is the author of it. fields.body_html:
But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness. ROMANS 4:5

Wesley’s opponents in the Church of England often accused him of neglecting good works. His Calvinist friends sometimes accused him of teaching that we are saved by them. Both were wrong, and the sermon that shows it most clearly is Justification by Faith, the fifth in his collected sermons. It is a calm, closely argued piece, and its answer to the oldest question of religion — how can a sinner be right with God? — is as clear as anything the Reformers wrote.

Two Adams

Wesley begins where Paul begins, with the two heads of the human race. By the sin of the first Adam, who was the father and representative of us all, we all fell short of the favour of God and became children of wrath. In the fullness of time Christ was made man, “a second general Parent and Representative of the whole human race.” He bore our sins in His own body on the tree, and by His sacrifice God has given the world a new covenant, whose plain condition being met, there is no more condemnation.

For as by one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous. ROMANS 5:19

This is the ground of the whole doctrine. We are not justified by our own obedience, but by the obedience of Another. Everything that follows depends on what Christ has done.

What justification is not

Wesley then clears away confusions, and it is characteristic of him that he spends as much time on what justification is not as on what it is.

It is not, first, the being made actually just and righteous. That is sanctification. Sanctification, he says, is indeed the immediate fruit of justification, but it is a distinct gift of God and of a totally different nature. Justification is what God does for us through His Son; sanctification is what He works in us by His Spirit. The two are never separated in experience, but they must not be confused in thought. If they are confused, people begin to think that God accepts them because they are becoming holy, and then they have lost the gospel.

Nor, secondly, does justification mean that God is deceived about us. It does not mean that He thinks us to be what we are not, or counts us righteous while pretending not to see our sin. God judges truly. He does not confuse us with Christ.

What justification is

What then is it? Wesley’s answer is plain: “The plain scriptural notion of justification is pardon, the forgiveness of sins.” It is that act of God the Father by which, for the sake of the propitiation made by the blood of His Son, He shows forth His righteousness by the remission of sins that are past. To the one who is justified, God will not impute sin. His sins are covered and blotted out, and he is accepted as though he had never sinned.

Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered. Blessed is the man unto whom the LORD imputeth not iniquity, and in whose spirit there is no guile. PSALM 32:1–2

This definition is deliberately simple. Wesley was suspicious of elaborate theories, and he wanted his hearers to grasp the main thing. When God justifies a sinner, He forgives him, fully and freely, and receives him into His favour.

Who are justified: the ungodly

The third question is the most startling. Who are the people God justifies? Wesley answers from his text: the ungodly. Not the good, not the religious, not those who have begun to reform themselves, but the ungodly of every kind and degree, and none but the ungodly.

This, he says, is why so many miss the gospel. They think they must first become holy and then be forgiven. But it is the sick who need a physician, and the lost whom the Shepherd seeks. It is not a saint whom God justifies, but a sinner. Holiness is the fruit of justification, not its condition.

They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick. MATTHEW 9:12

Wesley is careful here, because he knew the charge that such preaching encourages sin. But he would not soften the point. Whoever comes to God for pardon must come as a mere sinner, bringing nothing but ungodliness and pleading nothing of his own but sin and misery.

On what terms: faith alone

The fourth question is how the ungodly are justified, and the answer is: by faith alone. Justifying faith, Wesley says, is not only a conviction that God was in Christ reconciling the world to Himself, but “a sure trust and confidence that Christ died for ‘my’ sins, that he loved ‘me,’ and gave himself for ‘me.’” The personal pronouns carry the weight; he even marks them in the text. It is not enough to believe that Christ died for the world. The justified sinner trusts that He died for me.

I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me: and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me. GALATIANS 2:20

The moment God gives such faith, it is counted for righteousness. Faith is not a work that earns pardon; it is itself the gift of God. And why did God fix faith as the only condition? Wesley suggests one reason: to hide pride from man. Pride, he reminds us, destroyed the angels. God has chosen a way of salvation in which no one can boast.

The appeal

The sermon ends with one of Wesley’s great appeals, and it is worth hearing in its own voice. “Thou ungodly one, who hearest or readest these words! thou vile, helpless, miserable sinner! I charge thee before God, the Judge of all, go straight unto him, with all thy ungodliness.” Plead no works, he says, no righteousness of your own, no humility, contrition or sincerity. Plead only the blood of the covenant, the ransom paid for your proud, stubborn soul.

Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world. JOHN 1:29

Where to read with care

Some readers in the Reformed tradition have felt that Wesley was vague about the imputation of Christ’s righteousness, and he did at times hesitate over that phrase, fearing it could be used to excuse sin. His later sermon The Lord Our Righteousness shows that he held the substance of it, even if he was cautious about the language. And some of his followers were later less careful than he was in keeping justification distinct from sanctification. On the main question, though, this sermon stands with Paul, Augustine, Luther and the Anglican Homilies: we are accounted righteous before God only for the merit of our Lord Jesus Christ, by faith, and not for our own works or deservings.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Wesley says God justifies the ungodly. Do you still think you must become better before God will forgive you? Bring that thought to Him.

2. Write out Galatians 2:20 and underline every me. Pray it back to God as your own.

3. Distinguish in your own mind what God does for you in Christ and what He does in you by His Spirit. Thank Him for both.

4. Is there anything — your sincerity, your church-going, your repentance — that you have been pleading before God instead of Christ? Lay it down.

5. Read Justification by Faith in the Sermons on Several Occasions, and then read The Lord Our Righteousness beside it.

A PRAYER
Holy God, I come to You as I am, ungodly and with nothing to plead. I bring no works, no righteousness and no sincerity of my own.
I plead only the blood of Jesus, who was delivered for my offences and raised again for my justification.
Thank You that for His sake You forgive all my sins and receive me into Your favour. Let me not forget that He loved me and gave Himself for me.
Hide pride from me, and let all my boasting be in the Lord. Amen.

fields.title: The New Birth
fields.body_html:
Jesus answered and said unto him, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God. JOHN 3:3

When Wesley wanted to name the fundamental doctrines of Christianity, he named two. In his sermon The New Birth he says that if any doctrines may properly be called fundamental, “they are doubtless these two, — the doctrine of justification, and that of the new birth”. The first concerns the great work God does for us, in forgiving our sins; the second, the great work He does in us, in renewing our fallen nature. When he preached at Whitefield’s funeral he summed up his friend’s message in the same two phrases. The new birth was the heartbeat of the revival.

For us and in us

Wesley is careful about how justification and the new birth relate. In order of time, he says, neither comes before the other. In the very moment we are justified by grace through the redemption in Jesus, we are also born of the Spirit. But in order of thinking, justification comes first: we first conceive God’s wrath to be turned away, and then His Spirit to work in our hearts.

This matters because it guards two truths. The new birth is not the ground of our acceptance; we are not forgiven because we have been changed. But forgiveness is never without change. No one is justified who is not also born again, and no one is born again who is not also justified. The same moment brings both.

Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new. 2 CORINTHIANS 5:17

What the new birth is

To explain what the new birth is, Wesley follows Jesus’s own analogy. Before a child is born, he says, it has eyes but sees nothing, ears but hears nothing; it has scarcely any use of its senses and no knowledge of the world it is about to enter. So it is with the soul before it is born of God. It has spiritual senses, but they are closed. It does not see God, does not hear His voice, does not feel His love.

But when a person is born of God, all this changes. The eyes of the understanding are opened. He hears the inward voice of God saying, Be of good cheer, thy sins are forgiven thee. He feels the love of God shed abroad in his heart. And by a kind of spiritual respiration, as Wesley calls it in a companion sermon, grace descends into the soul and prayer and praise ascend to heaven, and the life of God in the soul is sustained.

Then comes his definition. The new birth is “that great change which God works in the soul when he brings it into life; when he raises it from the death of sin to the life of righteousness.” It is the change wrought in the whole soul by the Spirit of God, when the love of the world is changed into the love of God, pride into humility, passion into meekness, and hatred, envy and malice into a sincere and tender love for all mankind.

Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost. TITUS 3:5

Why it is necessary

Wesley gives three reasons why we must be born again. First, it is necessary for holiness, because gospel holiness is not a round of outward duties but “the image of God stamped upon the heart”, and that cannot begin until the heart is renewed. Second, it is necessary for eternal salvation, because without holiness no man shall see the Lord. Third, it is necessary for happiness, even in this world, because while pride, self-will and the love of the world reign in a soul, happiness has no place there.

Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord. HEBREWS 12:14

Not baptism, not sanctification

Wesley draws some careful inferences. First, baptism is not the new birth. He was an Anglican, and he accepted his Church’s teaching that infants baptised are at the same time born again. But he argues from the Church’s own catechism that baptism is the outward sign and the new birth the inward grace, and that the two can be separated. Whatever be the case with infants, he says, it is certain that not all of riper years who are baptised are born again; the tree is known by its fruits, and many continue servants of sin after baptism as before. In The Marks of the New Birth he tells such people bluntly to lean no more on the staff of that broken reed, that they were born again in baptism.

For he is not a Jew, which is one outwardly; neither is that circumcision, which is outward in the flesh: But he is a Jew, which is one inwardly; and circumcision is that of the heart. ROMANS 2:28–29

Second, the new birth is not the whole of sanctification. It is “the gate to it, the entrance into it.” As a child is born in a moment and then grows by degrees, so a person is born of God in a short time, if not in a moment, and then grows gradually to the stature of Christ. This distinction would become important in Wesley’s teaching on perfection.

The marks of the new birth

In a companion sermon, The Marks of the New Birth, Wesley sets out the signs by which a person may know he is born of God, and he takes them from Scripture: faith, hope and love. The faith is not a mere assent but a sure trust in God’s mercy through Christ, and its constant fruit is power over sin. The hope is a lively hope, the witness of the Spirit with our spirit that we are children of God. The love is love for God and for our neighbour, shown in keeping His commandments.

Beloved, now are we the sons of God, and it doth not yet appear what we shall be: but we know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is. 1 JOHN 3:2

Where to read with care

Wesley’s handling of baptism will satisfy neither those who think it has nothing to do with regeneration nor those who think it always effects it. He accepted that God regenerates infants in baptism, and also insisted that baptised adults living in sin must be born again. Readers will weigh that as their own traditions lead them. What he would not allow was any outward rite to take the place of an inward change. Go to church twice a day, he says, go to the Lord’s table every week, read ever so many good books: still, you must be born again.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Wesley calls justification and the new birth the two fundamental doctrines. Can you explain in your own words the difference between what God does for you and what He does in you?

2. Ask whether you are relying on any outward sign — baptism, membership, attendance — in place of an inward change.

3. Look for the marks of the new birth in your life: a trusting faith, a living hope, a practical love. Thank God for what you find, and ask for what is lacking.

4. The new birth is necessary for happiness. Where are you seeking happiness away from God?

5. If you are not sure you have been born again, pray the prayer Wesley gives at the end of The New Birth, asking God to deny you anything else rather than this.

A PRAYER
Lord, You have said that except a man be born again he cannot see Your kingdom. Do not let me rest in any outward thing.
If I have not been born of Your Spirit, give me this above all Your gifts. Take away whatever You please, but give me a new heart.
Open the eyes of my understanding, let me hear Your voice, and let me feel Your love shed abroad within me.
And let me grow from that new birth into the whole mind that was in Christ Jesus. Amen.

fields.body_html:
The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God. ROMANS 8:16

The thing Wesley received at Aldersgate was not a new doctrine but assurance: he felt that he did trust in Christ, and an assurance was given him that his sins were taken away. It is no surprise, then, that the witness of the Spirit became one of the characteristic teachings of the Methodist revival. Wesley preached on it more than once, and late in life he returned to the subject in a second discourse, saying that after twenty years’ further consideration he saw no cause to retract any part of what he had said. He called it one grand part of the testimony which God had given the Methodists to bear to all mankind.

Between two extremes

Wesley knew the doctrine was dangerous. He opens his sermon The Witness of the Spirit by lamenting how many vain people have wrested this very text to their own destruction, mistaking the voice of their own imagination for the witness of God’s Spirit and presuming they were God’s children while doing the works of the devil. These, he says, are enthusiasts in the worst sense of the word. But others, afraid of fanaticism, had explained the witness away altogether. Wesley asks whether we may not steer a middle course, keeping clear of enthusiasm without giving up the great privilege of God’s children. Surely we may.

Because ye are sons, God hath sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father. GALATIANS 4:6

Two witnesses

Wesley notices that Paul speaks of two witnesses: the Spirit Himself, and our spirit. The testimony of our own spirit is the testimony of conscience. We know from Scripture what the marks of God’s children are — love for God and our neighbour, obedience to His commandments — and when we find these in ourselves, our conscience bears witness that we are His. Wesley has a lovely way of putting how we know this. How do you know that you are alive, or that you are at ease and not in pain? You are immediately conscious of it. In the same way you may know that your soul is alive to God.

And hereby we do know that we know him, if we keep his commandments. 1 JOHN 2:3

But Paul says more than this. He says the Spirit Himself bears witness with our spirit. And Wesley insists that this is a direct testimony of God, not merely an inference we draw. His definition, which he offers with characteristic modesty, desiring any who are taught of God to correct or strengthen it, is this: “an inward impression on the soul, whereby the Spirit of God directly witnesses to my spirit, that I am a child of God; that Jesus Christ hath loved me, and given himself for me”, and that all my sins are blotted out and I am reconciled to God.

Why the Spirit’s witness comes first

Wesley argues that the witness of God’s Spirit must come before the witness of our own spirit, and his reasoning is simple and searching. We must be holy in heart and life before we can be conscious that we are. But we cannot be holy until we love God, and we cannot love God until we know that He loves us. And we cannot know His love for us until His Spirit witnesses it to our spirit.

We love him, because he first loved us. 1 JOHN 4:19

This is the pastoral heart of the doctrine. Wesley did not want people to build their assurance on their own progress in holiness, because that way lies either pride or despair. He wanted them to know first that they were loved, and then to love in return. The order matters, and it is the order of the gospel.

Telling the true from the false

How then can the true witness be distinguished from presumption and delusion? Wesley answers carefully, from Scripture.

First, Scripture describes repentance, or conviction of sin, as always going before the witness of pardon. The presumptuous person has never known a broken and contrite heart. Second, Scripture describes a great change as accompanying the new birth, from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God. Third, the joy that accompanies the true witness is a humble joy, one that abases a pardoned sinner to the dust; the proud spirit that cannot be humbled before God has not received the Spirit of Jesus. Fourth, it leads to obedience. The one who says he knows God and does not keep His commandments is a liar.

He that saith, I know him, and keepeth not his commandments, is a liar, and the truth is not in him. 1 JOHN 2:4

But how may one who has the real witness know it is not presumption? Wesley answers with a question. How do you distinguish day from night, or the light of a candle from the light of the noonday sun? There is an essential difference, and it is immediately perceived if our senses are rightly disposed. So it is with spiritual light. And the way to know that our spiritual senses are rightly disposed is by the fruit of the Spirit: love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness and the rest.

No witness without fruit

In the second discourse Wesley draws two inferences that summarise the whole teaching. The first is a warning: “let none ever presume to rest in any supposed testimony of the Spirit which is separate from the fruit of it.” If the Spirit of God truly witnesses that we are His children, the fruit of the Spirit will follow. The second is an encouragement: let none rest in any supposed fruit of the Spirit without the witness. There may be real foretastes of joy, peace and love, truly from God, long before a person is accepted in the Beloved; such a person should not rest in them until the Spirit witnesses with his spirit that his sins are forgiven.

But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, Meekness, temperance: against such there is no law. GALATIANS 5:22–23

Where to read with care

Wesley’s teaching on assurance was one of the most contested parts of his ministry, and some of the controversy was fair. In the early years he sometimes spoke as though no one could be justified without a clear, felt assurance, and he later softened this, recognising that many true believers have only a faint or intermittent sense of God’s witness. Readers who have never had a vivid experience of assurance should not conclude that they are not God’s children. Wesley himself came to distinguish the faith of a servant from the faith of a son, and to say that the former is accepted, though it should press on to the latter.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. On what do you rest your assurance that you are a child of God? Your feelings, your conduct, or the witness of God’s Spirit to His promises?

2. Read Romans 8:14–17 slowly, and ask the Spirit to bear witness with your spirit that you are God’s child.

3. Test your assurance by Wesley’s marks: repentance, a real change, humility, obedience and the fruit of the Spirit.

4. If you have only a faint sense of God’s love, do not despair; ask Him to make it clearer, and go on in obedience while you wait.

5. If you know someone troubled by doubt, share with them Wesley’s order: we love Him because He first loved us.

Abba, Father, thank You that You have sent the Spirit of Your Son into the hearts of Your children.
Let Your Spirit bear witness with my spirit that I am Your child, that Jesus loved me and gave Himself for me, and that my sins are blotted out.
Keep me from mistaking my own imagination for Your voice. Let the fruit of Your Spirit prove that the witness is true.
And because You first loved me, let me love You, and keep Your commandments with a glad heart. Amen.

fields.title: Sin Remains but Does Not Reign
fields.body_html:
For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other: so that ye cannot do the things that ye would. GALATIANS 5:17

Every new believer eventually meets the same bewildering discovery. The joy of forgiveness was real, the change was real, and for a while it seemed that sin itself had gone. Then it comes back: pride, anger, impatience, the old desires stirring again. Is the change not real after all? Was I deceived? Wesley met this question in thousands of people, and he answered it in two sermons that belong together: On Sin in Believers and The Repentance of Believers. They are among the most pastorally useful things he wrote, and they are essential for reading his teaching on perfection rightly.

The mistake of the young convert

Wesley describes the experience exactly in The Scripture Way of Salvation. Those who have been born again easily imagine that all sin is gone. They reason: I feel no sin, therefore I have none; it does not stir, therefore it does not exist. But it is seldom long before they are undeceived. Temptations return and sin revives, showing that it was only stunned, not dead. They now feel two principles in themselves, plainly contrary to each other: the flesh lusting against the Spirit.

A new doctrine resisted

That doctrine was the teaching, associated with the Moravian leader Count Zinzendorf and adopted by some in England, that true believers are delivered not only from the dominion of sin but from its very being, so that no sin at all remains in them from the moment they are justified. Wesley owed the Moravians a great deal; it was they who had shown him the way of faith. But on this point he opposed them firmly.

He appeals first to the whole body of ancient Christian writers, who with one voice declare that believers must still wrestle with an evil nature. He appeals to the Ninth Article of the Church of England, which says that the infection of nature remains even in the regenerate. And he appeals above all to Scripture, and particularly to Paul’s letters, where the grand point that there are two contrary principles in believers, the flesh and the Spirit, runs through them all.

And I, brethren, could not speak unto you as unto spiritual, but as unto carnal, even as unto babes in Christ. 1 CORINTHIANS 3:1

Wesley notices that Paul calls the Corinthians both carnal and babes in Christ in the same breath. They were believers, and yet in a degree they were carnal.

Guilt, power and being

The key to Wesley’s answer is a simple distinction. There is the guilt of sin, there is the power of sin, and there is the being of sin. “The guilt is one thing, the power another, and the being yet another.” Believers, he says, are delivered from the guilt and power of sin; they are not yet delivered from its being.

In the moment we are reconciled to God, the corruption of nature is put under our feet, and the flesh has no more dominion over us. But it still exists, though it does not reign. His summary line has become one of his best known: every babe in Christ is holy, and yet not altogether so. “It remains, though it does not reign.”

Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, that ye should obey it in the lusts thereof. ROMANS 6:12

Why it matters

Wesley saw two dangers in the opposite teaching. The first was despair. If a believer is told that no sin can remain in the regenerate, then the first time he feels pride or anger he will conclude that he was never born again, and he may cast away his confidence altogether. Wesley was protecting the weak.

The second danger was subtler. A believer who thinks there is no sin in him will see no need for continued repentance, and without repentance there is no way forward in holiness. In The Scripture Way of Salvation Wesley calls this the extreme mischievousness of a seemingly innocent opinion: by preventing repentance, it quite blocks up the way to sanctification.

The repentance of believers

This brings us to the second sermon. Most people think of repentance as something that happens at the start of the Christian life. Wesley agrees that there is a repentance that comes before faith. But he insists that there is also a repentance, and a faith, needed after we have believed, in every stage of our Christian course.

This later repentance is different from the first. It carries no sense of condemnation or fear of wrath. It is, he says, a conviction wrought by the Holy Spirit of the sin that still remains in the heart: a heart bent to backsliding, a propensity to pride, self-will, anger, love of the world. It is a conviction of the sin that still clings to our words and actions, even our best ones, which are mixed with evil in their spirit, matter or manner. And it is a conviction of our utter helplessness. We cannot, by all the grace we have, drive out the pride and self-will that remain in us.

O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death? I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord. ROMANS 7:24–25

And the faith that answers it

But Wesley does not leave believers there. To this repentance answers a faith: the conviction that Christ is able to save to the uttermost, and that He will cleanse the heart from all sin. The believer who knows his own helplessness is exactly the one ready to receive what God has promised.

Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them. HEBREWS 7:25

This is where Wesley’s teaching on perfection begins. It does not begin with a claim that believers are already sinless. It begins with an honest admission that they are not, a repentance that feels the remaining sin keenly, and a faith that looks to Christ to do what we cannot.

Reading this well

These two sermons are a gift to anyone discouraged by the persistence of sin after conversion. They say plainly: this is normal. Sin remaining in you is not proof that you are not a Christian. What matters is whether it reigns. Is it fought, confessed and hated, or is it served?

At the same time, they are a challenge to complacency. Wesley did not want believers to settle into a comfortable truce with remaining sin. He wanted them to repent of it daily, to feel their helplessness, and to trust Christ for more. The next chapters follow him along that road.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Have you been troubled by the return of old sins after conversion? Take comfort from Wesley: sin may remain where it does not reign.

2. Ask honestly whether any sin is reigning in your life — obeyed rather than resisted. Bring it to Christ today.

3. Practise the repentance of believers: ask the Spirit to show you one wrong temper still remaining in your heart.

4. Look at one of your best actions this week and notice what mixture of motive was in it. Confess it without despair.

5. Read Hebrews 7:25 and ask Christ, who is able to save to the uttermost, to do in you what you cannot do yourself.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You have delivered me from the guilt of sin and broken its dominion. Yet I still find in myself pride, self-will and a heart bent to backsliding.
Keep me from despair when I feel it, and keep me from making peace with it.
Give me the repentance of a believer, a clear sight of what remains, and a deep sense of my own helplessness.
And give me faith to trust You, who are able to save to the uttermost, to cleanse what I cannot cleanse. Amen.
