fields.body_html:
Who hath saved us, and called us with an holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given us in Christ Jesus before the world began. 2 TIMOTHY 1:9

If a reader wanted to read only one sermon of Wesley’s, this might be the one to choose. The Scripture Way of Salvation, published in 1765, is his mature summary of the whole Christian life, from the first dawn of grace to perfect love, and it is written with a clarity that makes it one of the finest short pieces of theology in English. It also shows how Wesley held together two things that are often set against each other: that salvation is entirely by faith, and that it is a life of growth in holiness.

Plain and simple

Wesley begins by noting how complicated religion has often been made to seem, and how plain and simple the genuine religion of Jesus Christ is when taken as Scripture describes it. The end it proposes is salvation; the means, faith. These two little words, he says, “include the substance of all the Bible, the marrow, as it were, of the whole Scripture.” So he asks three questions. What is salvation? What is the faith by which we are saved? And how are we saved by it?

Salvation is present

First, salvation is not what is often meant by that word, going to heaven. It is not a blessing on the other side of death. It is a present thing, a blessing which we are now in possession of. Taken in its widest sense, it includes everything God does in the soul from the first dawning of grace until it is consummated in glory: all the work of preventing grace, all the drawings of the Father and the convictions of the Spirit.

But in the narrower sense of the text, salvation consists of two general parts: justification and sanctification.

But now being made free from sin, and become servants to God, ye have your fruit unto holiness, and the end everlasting life. ROMANS 6:22

Justification, he says, is another word for pardon. It is the forgiveness of all our sins and our acceptance with God, procured by the blood and righteousness of Christ. Its immediate effects are the peace of God and a rejoicing in hope of the glory of God.

And at the same moment that we are justified, sanctification begins. We are born again, born from above; there is a real as well as a relative change. We feel the love of God shed abroad in our hearts, producing love to all mankind and expelling the love of the world, together with pride, anger and self-will.

Growth, and the goal

Then Wesley describes, with great realism, what follows. The new believer thinks sin is gone, and soon finds it only stunned. From the time of the new birth, he says, the gradual work of sanctification takes place. By the Spirit we mortify the deeds of the body, and as we are more and more dead to sin, we are more and more alive to God. We go on from grace to grace, abstaining from evil, zealous of good works, walking in all God’s ordinances, taking up our cross daily.

It is thus, Wesley says, that we wait for entire sanctification, a full salvation from all our sins. And he defines its heart in a sentence that deserves to be remembered: perfection “means perfect love. It is love excluding sin; love filling the heart, taking up the whole capacity of the soul.”

Rejoice evermore. Pray without ceasing. In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you. 1 THESSALONIANS 5:16–18

What faith is

Second, Wesley asks what faith is. In general, it is, as the writer to the Hebrews says, the evidence of things not seen: a divine evidence and conviction of the invisible things of God, a spiritual sight given by the Holy Spirit. In a more particular sense, it is a divine evidence and conviction not only that God was in Christ reconciling the world to Himself, but also that Christ loved me and gave Himself for me.

Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen. HEBREWS 11:1

The only condition

Third, how are we saved by faith? Here Wesley makes his central claim. “Faith is the condition, and the only condition, of justification.” No one is justified without faith, and everyone who believes is justified, whatever else he has or has not.

But does not God command repentance and its fruits too? Yes, Wesley answers, and they are necessary in some sense. But not in the same sense or degree as faith. The fruits of repentance are needed only if there is time and opportunity; the thief on the cross was justified without them. And repentance is needed only remotely, as a step toward faith, whereas faith is immediately necessary.

Then the surprise. Exactly as we are justified by faith, Wesley says, so we are sanctified by faith. His opponents had accused him for twenty-five years of teaching that we are sanctified by works. He had always said the opposite. “Faith is the condition, and the only condition, of sanctification, exactly as it is of justification.”

The place of works

Does this make works unnecessary? Not at all. Repentance and good works are necessary to sanctification in the same qualified way that repentance and its fruits are necessary to justification: they are the way in which God has appointed His children to wait for full salvation. And Wesley names them. First, works of piety: public, family and private prayer; the Lord’s Supper; searching the Scriptures by hearing, reading and meditating; and fasting as health allows. Second, works of mercy: feeding the hungry, clothing the naked, visiting the sick and imprisoned, instructing the ignorant, comforting the feeble-minded. The believer who wilfully neglects them cannot expect to grow in grace or even to keep what he has received.

And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not. GALATIANS 6:9

Expect it now

The sermon ends in a rising appeal. Does God work this great work gradually or instantaneously? It may be gradual in some, Wesley says, but it is desirable that it be instantaneous, and he believes God generally does it so. Therefore look for it every moment. And here is his test for whether you seek it by faith or by works: if by works, you want something done first; you think you must first be or do this or that. If by faith, you may expect it as you are, and expect it now. There is an inseparable connection, he says, between three points: “expect it by faith; expect it as you are; and expect it now!”

Behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation. 2 CORINTHIANS 6:2

Where to read with care

Wesley’s confidence that God generally sanctifies believers instantaneously is the part of this sermon most open to question. Scripture speaks of both decisive moments and long growth, and many mature Christians have known far more of the second than the first. Wesley himself allowed that the work may be gradual in some, and his followers who made an instantaneous second blessing the test of true holiness went beyond him. Read the sermon for its main lines: salvation is present, it includes both pardon and renewal, it comes by faith alone, and it bears fruit in works of piety and mercy. On those lines Wesley is on firm ground.

1. Wesley says salvation is a present thing. How does that change the way you think about your life this week?

2. Write down his two parts of salvation, justification and sanctification, and thank God for each in your own words.

3. Are you seeking holiness by works, waiting until you are better, or by faith, trusting Christ as you are? Be honest.

4. Choose one work of piety and one work of mercy from his lists that you have neglected, and do each this week.

5. Read The Scripture Way of Salvation in the Ochorus library in one sitting.

Thank You for pardon through the blood of Christ, and for the new life of Your Spirit that began in the same moment.
Let me go on from grace to grace, in prayer and Scripture and at Your table, and in works of mercy to all.
And let me look to You by faith, as I am, and now, for the love that fills the heart and casts out sin. Amen.

fields.title: Perfect Love
fields.body_html:
Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect. MATTHEW 5:48

No part of Wesley’s teaching has been more admired, more attacked or more misunderstood than his doctrine of Christian perfection. Late in life, in a letter, he called it the grand depositum which God had lodged with the people called Methodists, the particular truth they existed to keep alive. His enemies said it was pride dressed as piety. Some of his friends made it into something he never taught. And many modern readers, hearing the word perfection, assume at once that he meant something no honest person could believe. This chapter sets out what he actually taught; the next sets out, in his own words, what he did not.

Where it came from

Wesley’s own account is in A Plain Account of Christian Perfection, a short book he first published in 1766 and revised later, which is in the Ochorus library. It is partly a history of his own convictions and partly a collection of questions and answers from his Conferences.

He traces the doctrine back to 1725, when, at twenty-two, he read Jeremy Taylor’s Rules and Exercises of Holy Living and Dying and resolved to dedicate his whole life to God. The next year came Thomas à Kempis, and after that William Law. And from 1730, he says, he began to be homo unius libri, “a man of one book,” regarding none, comparatively, but the Bible. What he found there was a call to love God with all the heart and to be holy as God is holy, and he could not believe that such commands and promises were meant to remain empty.

On 1 January 1733 he preached before the University of Oxford a sermon called The Circumcision of the Heart, and in the Plain Account he points back to it as proof that his teaching had not changed. There he had defined the circumcision of the heart as “that habitual disposition of soul which, in the sacred writings, is termed holiness”, and he had said, with Paul, that love is the fulfilling of the law and the end of the commandment.

And the LORD thy God will circumcise thine heart, and the heart of thy seed, to love the LORD thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, that thou mayest live. DEUTERONOMY 30:6

What it is

What, then, is Christian perfection? Wesley’s answers are strikingly consistent, and strikingly simple. It is loving God with all our heart, mind, soul and strength, and our neighbour as ourselves. “It is nothing higher and nothing lower than this,—the pure love of God and man; the loving God with all our heart and soul, and our neighbour as ourselves.” In another place: “Pure love reigning alone in the heart and life,—this is the whole of scriptural perfection.” And in the short paper he added at the end of the book in 1767, Brief Thoughts on Christian Perfection: “By perfection I mean the humble, gentle, patient love of God, and our neighbour, ruling our tempers, words, and actions.”

Master, which is the great commandment in the law? Jesus said unto him, Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind. This is the first and great commandment. And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. MATTHEW 22:36–39

Notice the words: humble, gentle, patient. Wesley’s perfection is not a state of spiritual achievement that sets a person above others. It is love, and love of a very lowly kind. In the same book he warns that love is the highest gift of God, and that all visions, revelations and manifestations whatever are little things compared to it.

Why he believed it possible

Wesley’s argument was always from Scripture. God commands us to love Him with all our heart. He promises to circumcise our hearts to do so. Christ prayed that His people might be sanctified. Paul prayed that the Thessalonians might be sanctified wholly, and added that He who called them was faithful and would do it. John wrote that perfect love casts out fear, and that the blood of Jesus Christ cleanses from all sin. Wesley could not believe these were empty words.

And the very God of peace sanctify you wholly; and I pray God your whole spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless unto the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. Faithful is he that calleth you, who also will do it. 1 THESSALONIANS 5:23–24

He also pointed, gently, to the prayers of his own Church. In the Communion service Anglicans prayed every week that God would so cleanse the thoughts of their hearts by the inspiration of His Holy Spirit that they might perfectly love Him. Wesley asked simply whether they meant it.

How it comes

As the previous chapters have shown, Wesley taught that sanctification begins at the new birth and grows gradually. Believers are made more and more dead to sin and alive to God. But he also believed that God could, and often did, bring this work to a point of completion in a moment, cleansing the heart from sin and filling it with love. This, too, comes by faith, not by works. In the Brief Thoughts he says that this perfection “is always wrought in the soul by a simple act of faith”, and so in an instant, but with a gradual work both before and after.

If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. 1 JOHN 1:9

And he insists that it is not the end of growth. There is, he says, no perfection of degrees, none which does not admit of continual increase. The one who loves God with all his heart can love Him more tomorrow, as the heart itself is enlarged.

What it looks like

Wesley’s descriptions of the perfected Christian are full of the ordinary virtues. Such a person, he writes, rejoices evermore, prays without ceasing, and in everything gives thanks. He has been cleansed from pride and has put on bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness and longsuffering. Whether in ease or pain, sickness or health, life or death, he gives thanks from the ground of his heart to the One who orders all for good. He loves his enemies. He serves God with all his strength.

Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus. PHILIPPIANS 2:5

Why it matters

Whatever one concludes about Wesley’s more detailed claims, the heart of this teaching is a challenge the church cannot afford to ignore. Many Christians expect very little of the Christian life. They expect to be forgiven and to struggle, and they do not expect to be changed much. Wesley refused to accept this. He believed that God’s grace was greater than our sin, and that the love of God could fill a human heart and rule a human life, not only in heaven but here.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Read Wesley’s definition slowly: the humble, gentle, patient love of God and our neighbour, ruling our tempers, words and actions. Which of these words most searches you?

2. Do you expect God’s grace to change you deeply in this life, or only to forgive you? Ask Him to enlarge your expectation.

3. Pray the Communion collect this week, meaning every word: that God would cleanse the thoughts of your heart, that you may perfectly love Him.

4. Choose one relationship in which your love is impatient or proud, and ask God for His love to rule it.

5. Read the first few sections of A Plain Account of Christian Perfection in the Ochorus library.

A PRAYER
Almighty God, unto whom all hearts be open, cleanse the thoughts of my heart by the inspiration of Your Holy Spirit, that I may perfectly love You and worthily magnify Your holy name.
You have commanded me to love You with all my heart, and You have promised to circumcise my heart to do it. I believe You mean what You say.
Fill me with humble, gentle, patient love for You and for every person, and let it rule my tempers, my words and my actions.
And whatever measure of love You give me, let me always be growing in it, until I see You face to face. Amen.

fields.title: What Perfection Is Not
fields.body_html:
Not as though I had already attained, either were already perfect: but I follow after, if that I may apprehend that for which also I am apprehended of Christ Jesus. PHILIPPIANS 3:12

Wesley spent almost as much energy explaining what Christian perfection is not as explaining what it is. He had to. The word itself invited misunderstanding, and both his critics and some of his followers seized on it. His sermon Christian Perfection, on the text above, is built on this pattern: first, in what sense Christians are not perfect; then, in what sense they are. A Plain Account of Christian Perfection returns to the same distinctions again and again. Anyone who wants to be fair to Wesley, or to learn from him safely, must hear these qualifications in his own words.

Not perfect in knowledge

First, he says, Christians are not perfect in knowledge. They are not so perfect in this life as to be free from ignorance. Nor, second, are they free from mistake. “A man may be filled with pure love, and still be liable to mistake.” He may misjudge a fact or a person or the meaning of a text of Scripture.

Not free from infirmities or temptation

Third, Christians are not free from infirmities. By this Wesley means all those inward and outward imperfections that are not of a moral nature: weakness or slowness of understanding, confusion of thought, heaviness of imagination, slowness of speech, impropriety of language, and a thousand nameless defects of conversation or behaviour. These are found in the best of people. He is careful to say he does not mean what some people call their infirmities, such as drunkenness or taking God’s name in vain, which are simply sins given a gentler name.

Fourth, Christians are not free from temptation. Our Lord Himself was tempted, and the servant is not above his master. Still needing Christ

The most important qualification comes in the Plain Account, and it answers the charge that Wesley’s teaching made people independent of Christ. Every mistake, he says, is a transgression of the perfect law, and so even the most perfect Christian still needs the atoning blood. “The best of men still need Christ in his priestly office, to atone for their omissions, their short-comings”, their mistakes in judgement and practice, and their defects of various kinds.

Here Wesley makes a distinction that is vital for understanding him. There is sin, properly so called, which is a voluntary transgression of a known law. And there is sin improperly so called, which is an involuntary transgression of a divine law, known or unknown. Both need the atoning blood. But he believed that the first could be overcome by grace in this life, while the second remains until death. “I believe there is no such perfection in this life as excludes these involuntary transgressions”. And so he adds, famously: “Therefore sinless perfection is a phrase I never use, lest I should seem to contradict myself.”

Nor did Wesley believe that perfect love, once received, could not be lost. He says plainly in the Plain Account that it is exceeding common for people to lose it more than once before they are established in it. In his Brief Thoughts he explicitly retracts several expressions in the Methodist hymns that implied such an impossibility. And, as the previous chapter noted, he insisted that there is no perfection of degrees that does not admit of continual increase. Perfect love is not a summit where one sits down. It is a love that grows.

He also admitted uncertainty about when it usually comes. In the same Brief Thoughts he says that he believes the instant is generally the instant of death, though it may be ten, twenty or forty years before. That is a far more modest claim than many who came after him made.

The danger he saw most clearly

Wesley knew what could go wrong, because he saw it go wrong. In the Plain Account he describes how, in 1762, when there was a great increase of the work of God in London, enthusiasm broke in among some who professed perfection. Two or three began to take their own imaginations for impressions from God, and to suppose that they should never die; others fancied that they could not be tempted, that they would feel no more pain, and that they had the gift of prophecy. Some were soon got above instruction, and a handful of what he calls honest enthusiasts foretold that the world would end on a fixed day in February. They gave, he says, huge occasion of offence to those who opposed Christian perfection.

His response was a series of plain warnings to those who believed they had received perfect love. “Watch and pray continually against pride.” He points out that it is pride not only to ascribe to ourselves what we have, but to think we have what we have not. “Beware of that daughter of pride, enthusiasm.” Beware of judging others by your own feelings. Beware of antinomianism, of thinking that because you are filled with love you need not have so much holiness. Beware of self-indulgence, of censoriousness, of schism.

Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall. 1 CORINTHIANS 10:12

These warnings are among the wisest things Wesley wrote. They show that he did not imagine perfect love to be a safe place. It is the place where pride is most subtle and most dangerous.

Even with all these qualifications, many careful Christians have not been persuaded, and it is right to say why. Scripture calls sin whatever falls short of the glory of God, and many of the deepest saints have found themselves more aware of their sinfulness as they grew in grace, not less. Then said I, Woe is me! for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips. ISAIAH 6:5

fields.body_html:
Even from the days of your fathers ye are gone away from mine ordinances, and have not kept them. Return unto me, and I will return unto you, saith the LORD of hosts. MALACHI 3:7

A religion of grace can go wrong in two opposite directions. It can decay into formalism, in which people go through the motions of prayer, Scripture and sacrament as though the motions themselves could save. Or it can overreact into a contempt for all outward forms, as though the inward work of the Spirit made them unnecessary. Wesley met both errors, the first in the Church of England of his youth and the second among some of the very Moravians who had taught him the way of faith. His sermon The Means of Grace is his answer to both, and it shaped the daily life of Methodism for generations.

The quarrel over stillness

The occasion was a real controversy. In 1739 and 1740 some in the London society at Fetter Lane, under Moravian influence, began teaching that those who did not yet have true faith should be still: they should not pray, read the Scriptures or come to the Lord’s Supper, but simply wait for God, since using these means would only lead them to trust in their own works. Wesley saw where this led, and in 1740 he parted company with them.

In the sermon he treats the error with some sympathy. He acknowledges that the outward means had been terribly abused. Many had forgotten that the end of every commandment is love, and had made the means into the end. It was natural that sincere people, seeing this, should overreact. But the remedy for abuse is right use, not disuse.

What the means are

Wesley’s definition is clear and has been much quoted. “By ‘means of grace’ I understand outward signs, words, or actions, ordained of God, and appointed for this end, to be the ordinary channels whereby he might convey to men, preventing, justifying, or sanctifying grace.”

Notice each part. They are ordained of God, not invented by us. They are ordinary channels, the usual ways God works, though He is not bound to them. And they convey every kind of grace: the grace that awakens, the grace that justifies and the grace that sanctifies. They are not only for mature believers. They are for seekers too.

The chief of these means, he goes on, are prayer, whether in secret or with the great congregation; searching the Scriptures, which implies reading, hearing and meditating on them; and receiving the Lord’s Supper.

And they continued stedfastly in the apostles’ doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers. ACTS 2:42

Wait for grace in the means

Wesley’s central argument is that all who desire the grace of God are to wait for it in the means He has ordained, “in using, not in laying them aside.” And he proves it from Scripture, one means at a time.

Seekers are to wait for grace in prayer, because Christ says, Ask, and it shall be given you. They are to wait for it in searching the Scriptures, because Christ told even unbelievers to search them, since they testify of Him. And they are to wait for it at the Lord’s Supper, because Christ commanded, This do in remembrance of me.

Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you. MATTHEW 7:7

Wesley answers the objection that using the means is trusting in works. Not if they are used rightly, he says. The one who uses them as the way God has appointed, looking through them to God, is not trusting in himself but in God’s promise.

There is no power in this

At the same time, Wesley was just as concerned about the opposite error. He grants frankly that all outward means whatever, separated from the Spirit of God, cannot profit at all. And his directions for using them are a model of spiritual wisdom.

First, always remember that God is above all means. He can give grace without them, and He can withhold it through them. Second, before you use any means, let it be deeply impressed on your soul that there is no power in this. “The opus operatum, the mere work done, profiteth nothing”. There is no power to save but in the Spirit of God, and no merit but in the blood of Christ. Third, “In using all means, seek God alone.” Look through every outward thing to the power of His Spirit and the merits of His Son. Do not stick in the work itself. Nothing short of God can satisfy your soul.

Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts. ZECHARIAH 4:6

And lastly, after you have used any means, take care how you value yourself on it. To congratulate yourself on having done some great thing turns everything to poison. If God was not there, what did it avail? If He was, you will have forgotten, as it were, the outward work, because you will have seen that God is all in all.

Constant communion

Among the means, Wesley gave a special place to the Lord’s Supper, and here he was more of a high churchman than many of his evangelical contemporaries. In his sermon The Duty of Constant Communion, written first for his pupils at Oxford and published much later, he argues that it is the duty of every Christian to receive the Lord’s Supper as often as he can.

His reasons are two. First, it is a plain command of Christ. Second, its benefits are great: the forgiveness of our past sins and the present strengthening and refreshing of our souls. As our bodies are strengthened by bread and wine, so are our souls by these tokens of the body and blood of Christ. This, he says, is the food of our souls. He answers every excuse — unworthiness, lack of time, fear of making it common — and concludes that no one can claim to be a devout Christian who does not receive it as often as he can.

For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord’s death till he come. 1 CORINTHIANS 11:26

Wesley practised what he preached. His own diaries show him receiving Communion very frequently throughout his life, and he urged the Methodists to go to their parish churches for the sacrament.

Where to read with care

Wesley’s balance here is almost perfect, and the dangers are the ones he himself names. The reader from a sacramental tradition may be tempted to rest in the means; Wesley says there is no power in them apart from God. The reader from a free tradition may be tempted to despise them; Wesley says God has ordained them and we are to wait for Him there. Some may also question whether the Lord’s Supper should be offered to seekers who are not yet believers, as Wesley sometimes held; his practice on that point reflects his particular setting in a national church and has been debated since.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Which error are you more prone to: trusting in the forms, or neglecting them? Name it honestly.

2. Before your next time of prayer or Bible reading, pause and tell yourself: there is no power in this, but in God. Then seek Him alone.

3. After using a means of grace, notice whether you congratulate yourself. If so, give the praise to God.

4. Consider how often you receive the Lord’s Supper, and whether Wesley’s arguments ought to change your practice.

5. Read The Means of Grace in the Sermons on Several Occasions.

A PRAYER
Lord, You have given us prayer, Your Word and the Supper of Your Son as channels of Your grace. Forgive me when I have neglected them, and forgive me when I have trusted in them instead of You.
As I pray, speak with me. As I read, open my eyes. As I eat and drink, feed my soul with Christ.
Let me seek You alone in every means, and never rest in the work itself.
And when You meet me, let me forget myself and give You all the glory. Amen.

fields.title: Works of Piety and Works of Mercy
fields.body_html:
I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in: Naked, and ye clothed me: I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me. MATTHEW 25:35–36

From the days of the Holy Club, when the young Oxford Methodists visited prisoners in the Castle gaol and taught poor children to read, Wesley never separated prayer from practical love. He called the two works of piety and works of mercy, and he insisted that both belong to the way God has appointed for His children to grow. In two late sermons, On Zeal and On Visiting the Sick, he went further than most Christians of his day, or ours, would dare: he said that works of mercy are real means of grace, and that when they conflict with works of piety, mercy is to be preferred.

Two kinds of good works

In The Scripture Way of Salvation, as we saw, Wesley names both. Works of piety are prayer, public, family and private; receiving the Lord’s Supper; searching the Scriptures; and fasting. Works of mercy are those that relate to the bodies or souls of others: feeding the hungry, clothing the naked, entertaining the stranger, visiting the sick and the imprisoned, instructing the ignorant, awakening the careless, comforting the feeble-minded. Neither earns salvation. Both are the way in which a believer waits for God to complete His work.

Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world. JAMES 1:27

Mercy as a means of grace

In On Visiting the Sick Wesley challenges a common assumption. People generally suppose, he says, that the means of grace and the ordinances of God are the same thing: prayer, Scripture, the sacrament. “But are they the only means of grace?” His answer: “Surely there are works of mercy, as well as works of piety, which are real means of grace.”

The point is profound. Wesley believed that God meets us not only when we turn toward Him in worship, but when we turn toward our neighbour in need. The one who visits the sick, he says, gains an excellent means of increasing his thankfulness to God, and of increasing his sympathy with the afflicted, his benevolence and all his social affections. Whoever neglects it loses a means of grace.

He that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto the LORD; and that which he hath given will he pay him again. PROVERBS 19:17

Love on the throne

In On Zeal Wesley gives a picture of the Christian life that sets everything in its proper order, and it is one of the most useful images he ever offered. In a Christian believer, he says, love sits upon the throne erected in the inmost soul, the love of God and man, filling the whole heart and reigning without a rival. In a circle near the throne are all holy tempers: longsuffering, gentleness, meekness, fidelity, temperance. In an exterior circle are all the works of mercy, whether to the souls or bodies of men. fields.body_html:
And let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works: Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another. HEBREWS 10:24–25

Whitefield, it is often said, was the greater preacher, but Wesley’s converts lasted. Whether or not the comparison is fair to Whitefield, the reason behind it is real. Wesley did not preach and move on. He gathered those who were awakened into societies, divided the societies into classes, and gave every member a small circle of people who met weekly to ask how their souls prospered. He believed that the Christian life is not meant to be lived alone, and that the soul which has no one watching over it is in danger. This chapter looks at what he built and why.

How it began

Wesley tells the story himself in a late sermon, On God’s Vineyard. The early Methodist preachers, he says, had no plan at all. They simply went wherever they had a prospect of saving souls. But when more and more people came asking what they must do to be saved, they were desired to meet together. Twelve came the first Thursday night, forty the next, and soon a hundred. The London society grew to some thousands.

Then came a practical question: how should this multitude be kept together, and how should anyone know whether they walked worthy of their profession? The answer came, Wesley says, when they were thinking about something else entirely: paying off a debt. In Bristol in 1742 someone proposed dividing the society into small companies of about a dozen, each with a leader who would call on the members weekly to collect a penny for the debt. It was soon realised that the leader who called weekly could also inquire into their souls. The class meeting was born.

Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up. ECCLESIASTES 4:9–10

What the class meeting did

By this means, Wesley writes, “it was quickly discovered if any of them lived in any known sin.” Those who did were first admonished and, if they would not change, excluded from the society. Quarterly, the preacher examined every member and renewed their ticket of membership; exclusion was done quietly, by not renewing it.

That sounds severe, and it could be. But the heart of the class meeting was not discipline. It was care. Once a week, in a kitchen or a front room, a dozen ordinary people — miners, weavers, servants, shopkeepers — met with their leader, who asked each in turn how it was with their soul. They confessed their struggles, gave thanks for answered prayer, sang, prayed for one another, and went home knowing that someone would ask again next week. For thousands of people who had never had a pastor who knew their name, it was the first time anyone had asked.

Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much. JAMES 5:16

For those who wanted to go deeper, there were smaller bands, grouped by sex and marital status, which met for more searching confession. And the whole structure was held together by the annual Conference of preachers and by quarterly meetings of stewards and leaders.

The one condition

Wesley’s General Rules for the societies set only one condition for membership: a desire to flee from the wrath to come and to be saved from one’s sins. That was deliberately simple. No one had to prove his conversion or subscribe to a list of doctrines. But the rules went on to say how that desire would show itself: by doing no harm, by doing good of every possible sort, and by attending on all the ordinances of God. Those who continued in the society were expected to walk accordingly.

Wherefore comfort yourselves together, and edify one another, even as also ye do. 1 THESSALONIANS 5:11

This combination is worth noticing. The door was wide; anyone who wanted to be saved could come in. But once inside, people were expected to change, and others would help them.

Companions who watch over the soul

In On God’s Vineyard Wesley turns to those who had grown cold in the societies and asks why. One cause, he suggests, was their despising that excellent help, union with a Christian society. Have you not read, he asks, how can one be warm alone? And then a question worth putting to every Christian: you may have companions enough, perhaps more than enough, “But have you enough that are athirst for God, and that labour to make you so?” Have you companions “that watch over your soul, as they that must give account; and that freely and faithfully warn you, if you take any false step”?

Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful. PROVERBS 27:6

He also asks those who are members whether they make full use of the privilege: whether they never fail to meet their class, and do so not as a matter of form but expecting that when they meet in His name, the Lord will be among them.

Why it mattered

Wesley’s small groups did at least three things that preaching alone could not. They turned converts into disciples, giving them a place to grow and not only a moment of decision. They made pastoral care possible on a scale no clergy could manage, by putting it into the hands of ordinary believers; many class leaders were women. And they trained leaders. Men and women who had never spoken in public learned to pray aloud, to counsel, and eventually, some of them, to preach.

Bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ. GALATIANS 6:2

Where to read with care

The system also shows the weakness of its maker. Wesley governed the Methodist connexion with a firm and often autocratic hand. He appointed the preachers and moved them from circuit to circuit, admitted and excluded members, called the Conference and decided what it would discuss. He was usually wise and often generous, but he did not easily share authority, and critics within the movement complained of it. His famous defence of his power was that he had not sought it, and that those who submitted to it did so freely. That was true, but it left the movement poorly prepared for his death, and some of its later divisions trace back to the question of who should govern.

The class meeting, too, could decay. Where it lost its warmth, it became a form of inspection; where leaders were unwise, it could become intrusive. Wesley’s own question, whether people met as a matter of form or expecting Christ among them, is the test.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Ask Wesley’s question honestly: have you companions who watch over your soul and will faithfully warn you if you take a false step?

2. If you do not, name one or two believers you could invite to meet regularly to ask how your souls are prospering.

3. If you are in a small group, ask whether it meets as a matter of form or in expectation that Christ is present.

4. Practise James 5:16 this week: confess one struggle to a trusted brother or sister, and pray for each other.

5. Read On God’s Vineyard in Wesley’s Sermons on Several Occasions for his own account of the societies.

A PRAYER
Lord, You did not make me to be warm alone. Thank You for every brother and sister who has prayed for me, warned me and encouraged me.
Give me companions who thirst for You and who will watch over my soul, and make me such a companion to others.
Where I have hidden my struggles, give me courage to confess them. Where I have neglected fellowship, draw me back.
And when we meet in Your name, let us expect You in the midst of us. Amen.

fields.title: The Use of Money
fields.body_html:
And I say unto you, Make to yourselves friends of the mammon of unrighteousness; that, when ye fail, they may receive you into everlasting habitations. LUKE 16:9

Wesley’s three rules about money are among the few sentences of eighteenth-century theology that ordinary people still quote, though they usually quote only one or two of them and often in the wrong order. In his sermon The Use of Money, preached on the parable of the unjust steward, he reduces the whole Christian duty concerning money to three plain rules: gain all you can, save all you can, give all you can. Each rule is qualified, and the qualifications are the point. Together they make one of the most practical and most demanding sermons he ever preached.

Money is not evil

Wesley begins by refusing a common religious prejudice. Poets and philosophers, he says, have railed against money as the great corrupter of the world. But the fault lies not in money but in those who use it. Money can be used ill, and so can anything. It can also be used well. In the hands of God’s children, “it is food for the hungry, drink for the thirsty, raiment for the naked”. It gives the traveller and the stranger a place to lay his head. It can be a defence for the oppressed, a means of health to the sick, and of ease to those in pain.

For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows. 1 TIMOTHY 6:10

So the question is not whether a Christian should handle money, but how. And Wesley answers with his three rules.

Gain all you can

The first rule is a surprise from a preacher: gain all you can. Work hard. Use all possible diligence in your calling. Lose no time. Use common sense and all the understanding God has given you to do your work better today than yesterday.

But the rule is fenced at once. We must gain all we can without paying more for it than it is worth. We ought not to gain money at the expense of our life or health; no employment is worth that. Nor at the expense of our minds; we must not follow any trade that requires us to cheat or lie. And above all, not at the expense of our neighbour, in his substance, his body or his soul.

Here Wesley becomes very specific. We may not gain by ruining a neighbour’s trade to advance our own. We may not take such interest as the law forbids, or grow rich by gaming or by overgrown bills. He condemns pawnbroking as, on balance, doing more harm than good. And he denounces the trade in cheap distilled spirits, which he calls liquid fire, saying that those who sell them in the common way to anyone who will buy are poisoners. Nor may we gain by anything that corrupts the souls of others.

Woe unto him that buildeth his house by unrighteousness, and his chambers by wrong; that useth his neighbour’s service without wages, and giveth him not for his work. JEREMIAH 22:13

Save all you can

The second rule is save all you can, and Wesley means something different by it from what we usually mean. He does not mean hoard, or invest for security. He means do not waste. Do not throw away this precious talent, he says, in gratifying the desires of the flesh with delicate food, or the desire of the eye with expensive clothes, furniture and gardens, or the pride of life by buying the admiration of others. Every such expense, he says, not only wastes money but feeds the very desires that lead the soul away from God.

He has a sharp word too for parents who think they can never leave their children enough. Why should you leave them the means of increasing their sins? If a child is likely to waste an inheritance on folly, it would be kinder to leave him little.

Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal. MATTHEW 6:19

Give all you can

And then the third rule, without which the first two would be dangerous. Gaining and saving are not the end. “Having, First, gained all you can, and, Secondly saved all you can, Then ‘give all you can.’”

Wesley grounds this in stewardship. When God brought you into the world, he says, He placed you here “not as a proprietor, but a steward.” Everything you have is His, lent for a season. So first provide what is needful for yourself and your household. Then, if there is anything over, do good to those of the household of faith. And if there is still more, do good to all men. In so doing you give all you can; nay, in a sound sense, all you have. For all that is laid out in this manner is given to God.

Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful. 1 CORINTHIANS 4:2

He goes further than the tithe. Render unto God, he says, not a tenth, not a third, not half, but all that is God’s. And he offers four questions to test any expense: Am I acting herein as a steward and not a proprietor? Am I doing this in obedience to His Word? Can I offer this expense as a sacrifice to God through Christ? Have I reason to believe that for this very work I shall have a reward at the resurrection of the just?

The danger he foresaw

Wesley knew that his rules, if followed only in part, would produce a strange result. Methodists who worked hard and lived plainly would grow rich. And if they did not give, their riches would destroy them. In his last years he returned to this again and again. In On the Danger of Increasing Riches, preached in old age, he warns that unless charities increase in the same proportion as income, a person has set his heart on his gold. fields.body_html:
And when he was departed thence, he lighted on Jehonadab the son of Rechab coming to meet him: and he saluted him, and said to him, Is thine heart right, as my heart is with thy heart? And Jehonadab answered, It is. If it be, give me thine hand. 2 KINGS 10:15

It may seem strange that the man who wrote Free Grace also wrote Catholic Spirit, one of the most generous sermons on Christian unity in the English language. But the two belong together. Wesley held his convictions firmly and argued them hard, and he also believed, with equal firmness, that Christians who differ on important questions can and must love one another. Catholic Spirit, published in 1750, is his attempt to show how. The word catholic here does not mean Roman Catholic. It means universal: a spirit of love toward all who belong to Christ, whatever their church or opinions.

A strange text

Wesley’s text is an odd one. Jehu, the ruthless king who had just wiped out the house of Ahab, meets Jehonadab, and asks him only whether his heart is right. Wesley does not hold Jehu up as a model. He simply notices what Jehu did not ask. He did not inquire into Jehonadab’s opinions, though Jehonadab held some singular ones; his descendants were still keeping his peculiar rules centuries later. He asked only about his heart.

Why we cannot all think alike

Wesley begins with a realistic account of why Christians disagree. Love is due to all mankind, and a peculiar love to those who love God. Yet how many hindrances lie in the way! The two great hindrances are that Christians cannot all think alike, and in consequence cannot all walk alike, in their worship and practice.

He goes on to argue, with real humility, that this is inevitable. Every person necessarily believes that each of his own opinions is true, since to believe an opinion false is to cease holding it. And yet no one can be sure that all his opinions, taken together, are true. Everyone thinks he is right on each point; everyone must admit he is wrong on some, though he does not know which. Every wise person, therefore, will allow others the same liberty of thinking he desires for himself.

Who art thou that judgest another man’s servant? to his own master he standeth or falleth. ROMANS 14:4

Then comes the question at the centre of the sermon: “Though we cannot think alike, may we not love alike? May we not be of one heart, though we are not of one opinion? Without all doubt, we may.”

What it means to have a right heart

What then is Wesley asking when he asks, Is thy heart right, as my heart is with thy heart? Not whether you share his opinions or his forms of worship. He sets out instead a series of questions about the essentials. Is your heart right with God? Do you believe His being and His perfections? Do you believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, God over all, blessed for ever? Is He revealed in your soul? Do you know Him crucified? Do you walk by faith, not by sight? Is your faith filled with the energy of love? Do you love God? Do you love your neighbour, every person, even your enemies? Do you show your love by your works?

By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another. JOHN 13:35

If so, Wesley says, give me thine hand. And he explains what he means by that. “I do not mean, ‘Be of my opinion.’” Nor does he mean, embrace my modes of worship, or I will embrace yours. He means, first, love me, with a very tender affection, as a brother in Christ and a fellow soldier under the same Captain. Love me with the love that is patient and kind, that envies not if God prospers me more than you, that thinks no evil of me and puts the best construction on my words and actions. He means, second, commend me to God in all your prayers. Third, provoke me to love and good works. And fourth, love me not in word only, but in deed and in truth, and join me in the work of God as far as conscience allows.

What a catholic spirit is not

Wesley is careful to guard his teaching from misuse, and this part of the sermon is as important as the rest. A catholic spirit, he says, is not speculative latitudinarianism, an indifference to all opinions. The one who is unsettled, tossed about with every wind of doctrine, has not a catholic spirit but a curse. The person with a truly catholic spirit “is fixed as the sun in his judgement concerning the main branches of Christian doctrine.”

That we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine. EPHESIANS 4:14

Nor is it practical latitudinarianism, an indifference to forms of worship. Nor is it indifference to all congregations. The catholic Christian belongs to a particular church, is fixed in it, and worships there faithfully. His catholicity is not a lack of commitment. It is love reaching beyond his commitments.

A caution against bigotry

In a companion sermon, A Caution Against Bigotry, Wesley takes up the story of the disciples who forbade a man casting out devils in Jesus’s name, because he followed not with them. Jesus said, Forbid him not.

And John answered and said, Master, we saw one casting out devils in thy name; and we forbad him, because he followeth not with us. And Jesus said unto him, Forbid him not: for he that is not against us is for us. LUKE 9:49–50

Wesley applies this without hesitation. Suppose a man is not of our party, is separated from our church, and differs from us widely in judgement and practice. If we see him casting out devils, turning sinners from darkness to light, Jesus says, forbid him not. We must not hinder him, speak against him, or refuse to rejoice in the good God does through him.

Where to read with care

Wesley did not always live up to this sermon. His tone toward Calvinists, and in some writings toward Roman Catholics, fell short of it; he wrote sharply against Roman doctrine, and on the political question of toleration for Catholics he took positions many would now regret. The man who preached the catholic spirit was also a controversialist of his age. That is not a reason to dismiss the sermon, but it is a reason to read it as a standard he held up for himself as well as others, and did not always meet.

It is also worth noticing where he draws his lines. His questions about a right heart include the being and perfections of God, the deity of Christ, and trust in the righteousness of God by faith rather than in our own. Catholic Spirit is not an argument that doctrine does not matter. It is an argument that on the essentials we must be firm, on opinions we must be modest, and toward all who love Christ we must be warm.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Name a Christian or church with whom you differ on important but not essential matters. Pray for them by name this week.

2. Ask Wesley’s hard question of yourself: which of my opinions might be wrong, though I cannot yet see it?

3. Work through his questions about a right heart. Are you fixed as the sun on the main branches of Christian doctrine?

4. Is there anyone God is using whom you have been tempted to forbid because he follows not with you? Rejoice in the good he does.

5. Read Catholic Spirit in the Ochorus library, and share it with a friend from another tradition.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You prayed that Your people might be one. Forgive me for the pride that makes me despise those who do not think as I do.
Make me fixed in the great truths of the gospel, humble about my own opinions, and warm toward all who love You.
Where I cannot think alike with my brothers and sisters, let me love alike. Let me pray for them, provoke them to good works, and rejoice in all You do through them.
And bring us at last to the day when we shall know even as we are known. Amen.

fields.title: The World Is My Parish
fields.body_html:
And he said unto them, Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature. MARK 16:15

On 2 April 1739 a fastidious Oxford clergyman, who had once thought it almost a sin to save souls outside a church building, stood on a little rise of ground near Bristol and preached to some three thousand people in the open air. It was the beginning of fifty years of itinerant preaching that took Wesley across England, Wales, Scotland and Ireland, into market squares, graveyards, mining villages and the yards of inns. When he was challenged for intruding into other ministers’ parishes, his answer, recorded in his Journal, became the motto of the movement: “I look upon all the world as my parish.” This chapter asks what lay behind that sentence, and what it asks of us.

Plain truth for plain people

Wesley’s field preaching was not only a change of place. It was a change of audience, and it required a change of style. In the preface to his published sermons he explains that he had written them for the ordinary reader. “I design plain truth for plain people.” Of set purpose, he says, he abstained from all nice and philosophical speculations and intricate reasonings, and as far as possible from even the show of learning, and laboured to avoid all words not used in common life, especially the technical terms of the theologians, which to common people are an unknown tongue.

And my speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man’s wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power. 1 CORINTHIANS 2:4

This was costly for a man of his education. Wesley was a genuine scholar who read widely in several languages. But he laid it aside, or rather put it to work, so that miners and labourers could hear the gospel in words they understood. The same preface gives his reason in one of the most moving passages he wrote: he is a creature of a day, passing through life as an arrow through the air, and he wants to know one thing, the way to heaven. God has written it in a book. “O give me that book! At any price, give me the book of God!”

The gospel for those outside

Why did Wesley go to the fields? Because the people were there, and they were not in church. The industrial and mining communities growing up in England were often far from any parish church, or unwelcome in it. Many had never heard the gospel preached with any urgency. The respectable clergy, with some honourable exceptions, did not go to them. Whitefield did, and Wesley followed.

Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in hither the poor, and the maimed, and the halt, and the blind. LUKE 14:21

In Salvation by Faith he had already argued that the poor have a peculiar right to have the gospel preached to them. Field preaching was that conviction put into practice. It was also, often, dangerous. Wesley was stoned and struck, dragged through mobs, and threatened with death. His Journal records these things with a strange calm, and many of those who came to mock stayed to pray.

Christianity spreading

Wesley’s hope for the gospel was large. In his sermon Scriptural Christianity, preached before the University of Oxford in 1744, he describes Christianity in three stages: as beginning in individual hearts at Pentecost, as spreading from one to another, and as finally covering the earth. It is a picture of a whole society transformed by love. Then, in a plain, practical application, he turns on his hearers and asks, in tender love, whether Oxford is a Christian city at all. He was never invited to preach there again.

For the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea. HABAKKUK 2:14

Late in life, in The General Spread of the Gospel, he looked at the world as it then was, largely unreached, and refused to despair. He traces how the little leaven of living religion had spread from a handful at Oxford across Britain, Ireland and America, and he looks forward to its spreading further still. And he describes how God works: not usually by sudden spectacular means, but as the kingdom “will silently increase, wherever it is set up, and spread from heart to heart, from house to house, from town to town, from one kingdom to another.”

Lay preachers

The call of the world as parish also led Wesley to one of his most controversial decisions. Ordained clergy who shared his views were few, and most were settled in parishes. The work was growing beyond what they could do. And so he began, at first reluctantly, to allow laymen to preach. In On God’s Vineyard he describes how, when no clergyman dared to help, one and another, though not ordained, offered to assist, and God gave a signal blessing to their word. Some were learned and some unlearned, most were young, but it pleased God to own them all.

Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marvelled; and they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus. ACTS 4:13

These lay preachers, travelling in circuits and moved every year or two, carried Methodism into every corner of the land and eventually across the Atlantic. Wesley’s willingness to trust ordinary men, and in some cases women, with the gospel was one of the reasons the revival lasted.

Where to read with care

The world as parish carried Wesley across church boundaries in ways the Church of England found hard to accept, and in the end it led, after his death, to separation. He himself never intended to leave the Church, and he told his people to attend their parish churches and receive the sacrament there. But his ordinations for America in 1784, and the independence of his societies, made the separation almost inevitable. Readers will judge that history differently. What is clear is that his first loyalty was to the souls of those the church was not reaching, and that the church he loved often made it hard for him to serve them within it.

It should also be said that the romance of field preaching can hide its cost to those at home. Wesley’s constant travelling was one of the causes of his unhappy marriage. Zeal for the world is no excuse for neglecting those nearest to us.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Where are the people in your town who would never come to church? Pray for them by name or by place this week.

2. Is there a preference or habit that keeps you from going where people are? Ask God whether He wants you to lay it down.

3. Practise plain truth for plain people: try to explain the gospel in a few sentences without any religious jargon.

4. Pray for the spread of the gospel from heart to heart and house to house in your neighbourhood.

5. Read the preface to Wesley’s Sermons on Several Occasions and Scriptural Christianity in the Ochorus library.

A PRAYER
Lord of the harvest, You sent Your disciples into all the world. Give me Your love for those who are outside, who have never heard, or who have heard and never cared.
Make me willing to go where people are, and to speak plainly of Your grace in words they understand.
Raise up ordinary men and women to carry Your gospel, and let it spread silently from heart to heart and house to house.
Keep me faithful to those nearest me, even as You send me to others. Amen.

When he was challenged for intruding into other ministers’ parishes, his answer, recorded in his Journal, became the motto of the movement: “I look upon all the world as my parish.” This chapter asks what lay behind that sentence, and what it asks of us. Plain truth for plain people Wesley’s field preaching was not only a change of place. It was a change of audience, and it required a change of style. In the preface to his published sermons he explains that he had written them for the ordinary reader. “I design plain truth for plain people.” Of set purpose, he says, he abstained from all nice and philosophical speculations and intricate reasonings, and as far as possible from even the show of learning, and laboured to avoid all words not used in common life, especially the technical terms of the theologians, which to common people are an unknown tongue. Wesley was a genuine scholar who read widely in several languages. But he laid it aside, or rather put it to work, so that miners and labourers could hear the gospel in words they understood. The same preface gives his reason in one of the most moving passages he wrote: he is a creature of a day, passing through life as an arrow through the air, and he wants to know one thing, the way to heaven. God has written it in a book. “O give me that book! At any price, give me the book of God!” The gospel for those outside Why did Wesley go to the fields? It was also, often, dangerous. Wesley was stoned and struck, dragged through mobs, and threatened with death. His Journal records these things with a strange calm, and many of those who came to mock stayed to pray. Christianity spreading Wesley’s hope for the gospel was large. In his sermon Scriptural Christianity, preached before the University of Oxford in 1744, he describes Christianity in three stages: as beginning in individual hearts at Pentecost, as spreading from one to another, and as finally covering the earth. It is a picture of a whole society transformed by love. Then, in a plain, practical application, he turns on his hearers and asks, in tender love, whether Oxford is a Christian city at all. He was never invited to preach there again. For the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea. He traces how the little leaven of living religion had spread from a handful at Oxford across Britain, Ireland and America, and he looks forward to its spreading further still. And he describes how God works: not usually by sudden spectacular means, but as the kingdom “will silently increase, wherever it is set up, and spread from heart to heart, from house to house, from town to town, from one kingdom to another.” Lay preachers The call of the world as parish also led Wesley to one of his most controversial decisions. Ordained clergy who shared his views were few, and most were settled in parishes. The work was growing beyond what they could do. And so he began, at first reluctantly, to allow laymen to preach. In On God’s Vineyard he describes how, when no clergyman dared to help, one and another, though not ordained, offered to assist, and God gave a signal blessing to their word. Some were learned and some unlearned, most were young, but it pleased God to own them all. Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marvelled; and they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus. He himself never intended to leave the Church, and he told his people to attend their parish churches and receive the sacrament there. But his ordinations for America in 1784, and the independence of his societies, made the separation almost inevitable. Readers will judge that history differently. What is clear is that his first loyalty was to the souls of those the church was not reaching, and that the church he loved often made it hard for him to serve them within it. It should also be said that the romance of field preaching can hide its cost to those at home. Wesley’s constant travelling was one of the causes of his unhappy marriage. Zeal for the world is no excuse for neglecting those nearest to us. FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION 1. Where are the people in your town who would never come to church? Pray for them by name or by place this week. 2. Is there a preference or habit that keeps you from going where people are? Ask God whether He wants you to lay it down. 3. Practise plain truth for plain people: try to explain the gospel in a few sentences without any religious jargon. 4. Pray for the spread of the gospel from heart to heart and house to house in your neighbourhood. 5. Read the preface to Wesley’s Sermons on Several Occasions and Scriptural Christianity in the Ochorus library. A PRAYER Lord of the harvest, You sent Your disciples into all the world. Give me Your love for those who are outside, who have never heard, or who have heard and never cared. Make me willing to go where people are, and to speak plainly of Your grace in words they understand. Raise up ordinary men and women to carry Your gospel, and let it spread silently from heart to heart and house to house. Keep me faithful to those nearest me, even as You send me to others. Amen.

fields.title: The Poor and the Slave
fields.body_html:
Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction. Open thy mouth, judge righteously, and plead the cause of the poor and needy. PROVERBS 31:8–9

Wesley’s gospel was not only for the soul. He believed that the love of God, once it fills a heart, must overflow toward everyone that heart can reach, and especially toward those whom the world passes by. Across his long life that love took practical shape in schools, medicine, loans, visits to prisons and workhouses, and at the last in a public campaign against the slave trade. This chapter gathers those threads. It is the place where his teaching on perfect love, on works of mercy and on the use of money comes out into the street.

Holiness is never solitary

Wesley is remembered as saying, in the preface to one of the early Methodist hymn books, that the gospel of Christ knows no holiness but social holiness. In context he was arguing against a solitary religion of the desert, insisting that holiness grows in fellowship and not in isolation. But the principle reaches further than that. The love that Wesley preached could not be kept inside the society meeting. It had to reach the neighbour, and the neighbour, as he says in The Almost Christian, is every man in the world.

Hereby perceive we the love of God, because he laid down his life for us: and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren. But whoso hath this world’s good, and seeth his brother have need, and shutteth up his bowels of compassion from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him? 1 JOHN 3:16–17

Among the poor

The Methodist societies were overwhelmingly societies of the poor, and Wesley spent his life among them. From the Holy Club onward he visited prisoners, and he preached to condemned men in their cells. He set up a school for the children of the colliers at Kingswood near Bristol. In London he organised collections for the poor, found work for the unemployed, and established a small lending fund so that people could borrow without falling into the hands of moneylenders. He opened a dispensary where the sick could receive simple remedies, and he wrote a book of cheap and practical medicine, Primitive Physic, for people who could not afford a physician.

None of this was separate from his preaching. It flowed from the same conviction: that the love of God must show itself in works of mercy, and that those who have more are stewards of it for those who have less. His sermon On Visiting the Sick, as we saw, insists that the rich must go to the poor in person. And in his sermon On Dress he denounces expensive clothing in words that still sting. He begs his hearers not to lay out on nothing “what may clothe your poor, naked, shivering fellow-creature!” And then: “Everything about thee which cost more than Christian duty required thee to lay out is the blood of the poor!”

He that oppresseth the poor reproacheth his Maker: but he that honoureth him hath mercy on the poor. PROVERBS 14:31

Who cares for the Africans

Wesley’s concern for the enslaved went back to his time in the American colonies, where he had seen slavery at first hand. In his sermon The Imperfection of Human Knowledge, reflecting on the mysteries of providence, he asks who cares for the millions of Africans who are continually driven to market and “sold, like cattle, into the vilest bondage”, with no hope of deliverance but death. It is a cry of grief that he cannot answer.

In 1774 he did more than grieve. After reading the work of the Quaker Anthony Benezet, he published Thoughts upon Slavery, one of the earliest and most forceful attacks on the slave trade by a leading English churchman. In it he described the capture of Africans, the horrors of the voyage and the cruelty of the plantations. He answered the arguments of those who said the trade was necessary for commerce or legal under English law, denying that any law could make right what is contrary to justice and mercy. He insisted that slave-holding could not be squared with even natural justice. And he addressed himself directly to the ship captains, the merchants and the planters, urging each of them to give up the trade, whatever it cost them.

He that stealeth a man, and selleth him, or if he be found in his hand, he shall surely be put to death. EXODUS 21:16

The last letter

Wesley kept up the cause to the end. In February 1791, only days before his death, he wrote to William Wilberforce, the young Member of Parliament who was leading the campaign in the House of Commons against the slave trade. He urged him not to be weary in well-doing, warned him that unless God had raised him up for this very thing he would be worn out by opposition, and encouraged him that if God was for him, none could be against him. He called the trade a villainy that was the scandal of religion, of England and of human nature. It is among the last letters of his that survive. The slave trade was abolished in the British Empire in 1807, and slavery itself in the 1830s, and the Methodist people, in Britain and beyond, were among the campaign’s most faithful supporters.

And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not. GALATIANS 6:9

Where to read with care

It would be easy to make Wesley a modern social reformer, and he was not. He did not question the structure of eighteenth-century society in most respects. He was a loyal Tory who opposed the American Revolution. His charity, though generous, was usually personal rather than political, and some of his descriptions of the poor and of other peoples carry the condescension and prejudice of his age. The same sermon that grieves over the enslaved Africans speaks of them, and of other peoples, in terms no Christian should repeat. It is honest to say so.

But it is also honest to say that on the greatest moral question of his century he saw clearly and spoke plainly, when many churchmen, including many good ones, were silent or complicit. And his reasons were not those of a political programme. They were the reasons of the gospel: that every human being bears the image of God, that Christ died for all, and that love for God is a lie if it can look on a brother’s chains and do nothing.

Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke? ISAIAH 58:6
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Wesley believed that holiness is never solitary. How does your love for God reach the people around you, especially the poor?

2. Look at one thing you own or plan to buy, and ask Wesley’s hard question: did it cost more than Christian duty required?

3. Learn about one form of modern slavery or exploitation, and find one practical way to oppose it.

4. Is there a moral question on which the church around you is silent? Ask God whether He is calling you to speak.

5. Pray for those who campaign for justice today, as Wesley encouraged Wilberforce, that they will not grow weary.

A PRAYER
Father of all, You made every human being in Your image, and Your Son died for all. Forgive us for the times we have looked away from the poor and the oppressed.
Let the love You pour into my heart overflow toward my neighbour, whoever and wherever he is.
Give me courage to open my mouth for those who cannot speak for themselves, and wisdom to act, not only to feel.
Strengthen all who labour against injustice, that they may not be weary in well-doing, and let Your kingdom come on earth as it is in heaven. Amen.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
Now the end of the commandment is charity out of a pure heart, and of a good conscience, and of faith unfeigned. 1 TIMOTHY 1:5

We began with a sentence: the grace that pardons is the grace that heals. It is worth looking back to see how far that one conviction has carried us.

Wesley looked at human nature and saw a disease: pride, self-will, love of the world, a heart turned away from God. He looked at the gospel and saw a cure. God goes before us with grace, stirring conscience and good desires before we ever seek Him. He justifies the ungodly freely, for Christ’s sake, the moment they believe. In the same moment He gives them a new birth and, by His Spirit, witnesses to them that they are His children. And then He goes on working, through prayer and Scripture and the Lord’s Supper, through fellowship and works of mercy, until love for Him and for our neighbour fills the heart and rules the life.

Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ. PHILIPPIANS 1:6

What he gives us

Wesley gives the church at least four gifts that it keeps needing to receive again.

The first is the refusal to separate faith and holiness. Some Christians preach faith and forget that it must change us. Others preach holiness and forget that it comes by grace. Wesley held both with equal force. We are saved by faith alone, and the faith that saves is never alone; it works by love.

The second is assurance. Wesley knew what it was to be a disciplined, sincere, orthodox Christian without the knowledge that God loved him. He wanted no one else to live that way. The witness of the Spirit, guarded by Scripture and tested by its fruits, is one of the great comforts of the Christian life, and he taught the church to expect it.

The third is a high expectation of grace. Whatever we make of his more detailed claims about perfection, Wesley believed that God could do far more in a human heart than most Christians dare to hope. He would not accept that the Christian life is only forgiveness and struggle. He preached perfect love as the goal, and he sent people after it with all their hearts.

The fourth is a Christianity that goes outward. He took the gospel to the fields and the mining villages, gathered the converts into small groups where they watched over one another, taught them to gain, save and give, sent them to visit the sick and the prisoner, and at the last lifted his voice against the slave trade. For Wesley, love that stayed inside a meeting room was not love at all.

Let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth. 1 JOHN 3:18

What to leave behind

This book has tried to be honest about the places where Wesley must be read with care. His language about perfection sometimes ran ahead of his own careful qualifications, and those who followed him did not always keep the qualifications. His controversy with the Calvinists was conducted with more heat than fairness, even though his friendship with Whitefield survived it. His leadership of the movement was often autocratic. His marriage was unhappy, and he bears part of the blame. He was a man of his time on many questions, and some of his words about other peoples are painful to read.

The best of all

Near the end of his life, those at his bedside remembered him saying, more than once, that the best of all is that God is with us. It is a fitting summary. For all his energy, all his organisation, all his miles and sermons and societies, Wesley’s message was not finally about what we do. It was about what God does: that He comes to us, forgives us, lives in us and loves through us. The Christian life begins with grace and goes on by grace, and its end is love.

Beloved, let us love one another: for love is of God; and every one that loveth is born of God, and knoweth God. 1 JOHN 4:7

The best way to honour Wesley is not to admire him but to go where he pointed. Go to Christ in faith. Use the means He has given. Find companions who will watch over your soul. Visit the sick and give to the poor. And expect God to fill your heart with His love, as you are, and now.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Look back over the chapters of this book. Which one teaching of Wesley’s has most searched or helped you?

2. Ask whether you have separated faith and holiness in your own life, and in which direction you lean.

3. Choose one practical step from these pages — a small group, a visit, a change in giving — and take it this month.

4. Name one caution from this book that you need to keep in mind as you read Wesley for yourself.

5. Decide which of his sermons you will read next, and when.

A PRAYER
Gracious God, You went before me with Your grace, You pardoned me for Christ’s sake, and You have begun to make me new. Finish the work You have begun.
Thank You for Your servant John Wesley, for all that was faithful in his teaching and his life, and forgive what was not.
Give me faith that works by love, companions who will help me on the way, and a heart that goes out to the poor and the lost.
Fill me with Your love until it rules my tempers, my words and my actions. And let me know, all my days, that the best of all is that You are with us. Amen.
